CHR, a declarative language for writing efficient solvers, has seen various extensions emerge, with multi-headed logic marking a significant milestone. This study investigates the implications of incorporating multi-head concurrent subgoals in CHR, measuring the impact on its expressiveness. We demonstrate that a particular type of multi-head concurrent subgoal can be expressed through a more constrained form, specifically by the use of multi-head concurrent subgoals featuring a separation marker. The outcome suggests that the multi-head concurrent subgoals offer enhanced expressiveness compared to their one-headed counterparts, resulting from their ability to process subgoals simultaneously, ultimately reducing the number of rule applications required during solving processes.

Galaxy rotation direction can be determined by observing the orientation of spiral arms through the inner isophote's rotation position. Two previous studies found a correlation between galaxy shape and the counter-clockwise rotation direction at low redshifts. This study examines the shape of around 1.3 million galaxies from the Dark Energy Survey using the S4G catalog comparison, with the goal of understanding the shape's impact on galaxy formation. The research found a strong correlation between the shape and counter-clockwise rotation direction at low redshifts. This study also analyzed data from four other sky surveys, each containing around 1.3 million galaxies, to confirm the observed counter-clockwise rotation trend. The results, however, show inconsistencies in the shape classifications across the surveys, with concerns about observer bias.

Meta-learning has made significant advancements in few-shot learning, but its resilience to real-world conditions is underexplored. To address this, we've developed Eigen-Reptile, a novel algorithm designed to improve the robustness of meta-learning in challenging environments. By utilizing a novel form of Bayesian lower bound optimization, Eigen-Reptile minimizes the impact of data corruption during the meta-learning process. Our theoretical analysis reveals that Eigen-Reptile can effectively recover model parameters even when faced with corrupted labels in new tasks, and our experiments show significant gains in robustness compared to state-of-the-art methods across various image classification and object detection scenarios.

A major challenge in the analysis of medical images lies in creating detailed, accurate maps that highlight specific features, such as brain abnormalities. Existing techniques fall short in this area, as they either focus solely on local features or fail to provide reliable results. Our approach, ICAM-reg, overcomes these limitations by producing accurate, interpretable and locally precise intensity maps. This is achieved through a novel method that utilizes a modified U-net architecture, incorporating a regression loss function to improve results and an attention mechanism for enhanced feature extraction. Our technique was tested on 46 multiple sclerosis scans and proved effective in creating high-accuracy, interpretable and locally precise feature maps, making it a valuable tool for disease analysis. Our results were found to align well with clinical expert interpretations of the brain scans.

The current AI ethics landscape is marked by a multitude of frameworks, principles, and guidelines, but the integration of these perspectives into actual practice remains limited. A key challenge arises when bridging the gap between theoretical frameworks and implementation, driven by the influence of influential stakeholders, is hindered by the absence of diverse inputs. Furthermore, the lack of participation by marginalized communities in the development of AI ethics is evident, as their voices are often silenced and their concerns at times even exploited. To address these issues, we highlight the need for co-design as a promising approach to incorporate marginalized perspectives and facilitate the adoption of AI ethics within real-world systems, exemplified by the co-design efforts of the AI for Social Good community.

This study examines language families that include $\omega$-regular languages and are extended by the ability to utilize non-deterministic choices along infinite words. Three such families are investigated: those that use a fixed number of choices, an unlimited number of choices, and a variable number of choices greater than one. Theoretical work on these families is compiled, and existing research is refreshed with the aim of providing a clear and accessible overview of the subject.

A cutting-edge downlink cell-free massive MIMO (mMIMO) system is proposed, leveraging channel estimation and forecasting to improve performance in time-variant environments without additional overhead. By utilizing an advanced alternating deep neural network, channel gain and channel aging can be accurately determined, resulting in enhanced SE up to 30% with reduced feedback overhead. The proposed framework's efficiency is proven through comparison with conventional methods that rely on pilot symbols, demonstrating its ability to support high-speed mMIMO systems with large coherent periods and fast fading.

We calculate the electromagnetic corrections for the semi-leptonic kaon decays $\mathcal{K}^{+,\,0} \to \mathcal{π}^{0,\,+}$ using a detailed model of the nucleons and their associated photons. The model accounts for the finite size of the particles as well as their substructure derived from recent lattice simulations. The derived values for the electromagnetic modifications to the weak matrix elements $|V_{ud}|$ are found to be $|V_{ud}| = 0.4701(60)$ and $|V_{ud}| = 0.4765(63)$, respectively. These values are in agreement with existing estimates derived from measurements of the neutron decay and nuclear beta decay.

We present a novel image denoising network, Identity Boosted Residual Image Denoising (IBRID), which utilizes a convolutional neural network to remove noise from an input image. Our approach is built upon a residual denoising network (RED), which we improved using an efficient technique to boost network performance. The Riesz transform, used as a spatial gradient filter, helps to locate noise in complex images and can be used as a thresholding algorithm in the denoiser network. We initially train our network on a subset of the synthetic image dataset from the CVPR 2017 challenge and then fine-tune it using a substantial real-world image dataset to significantly enhance its denoising performance. Our proposed IBRID network outperforms other top-performing models in the field, as evidenced by our experimental results.

Multiview learning has emerged as a powerful strategy for enhancing representation and generalization capabilities of neural networks, with a significant proportion of multiview methods built upon latent correlation-based approaches. These approaches, which rely on latent representations that correlate across different views, offer advantages like reduced computational and memory requirements, making them more practical compared to traditional multiview methods. Notably, many latent correlation-based methods are self-guided, meaning they incorporate the learned representations into their loss functions. However, a critical gap exists in understanding the effectiveness of these approaches, which is addressed by examining them under a unified framework of identifiability. Specifically, we show that latent correlation-based approaches can be viewed as a general class of multiview learning methods that leverage the distinctiveness of labels across multiple views. This framework enables us to clarify the underlying principles of latent correlation-based approaches, derive novel self-guided multiview methods, and provide theoretical justifications for their efficacy.

We've analyzed a dataset of infrared and optical galaxy observations to identify objects exhibiting unusual properties. Our selection criteria identified objects whose colours don't match the typical trends in their environment, and we've found that these objects are distinct from typical star-forming galaxies. Instead, they appear to be a mix of galaxies with reduced star formation, galaxies undergoing massive galaxy mergers, and active galactic nuclei. Further examination suggests that these objects primarily consist of AGN and mergers with varying levels of dust. The classification of these objects as AGN is supported by their mid-infrared and X-ray properties, while classification as mergers is complicated by the challenges of distinguishing between ongoing and post-m merger systems. Notably, the red colour of these objects is primarily the result of dust properties rather than the presence of hot, young stars.

As AI systems increasingly perform tasks akin to human capabilities, traditional measures of task success are no longer sufficient for assessing their value, as this depends on user-specific moral standards. Given that these moral standards sometimes conflict with AI rules, it is crucial to develop methods that capture the user's moral judgment in evaluating the AI's performance. In this research, we introduce a new method that measures the user's moral judgment in evaluating the AI's actions through an approach inspired by moral rule theories. Our approach focuses on identifying the underlying principles of the user's moral judgment, which can be used to predict whether the AI should adhere to certain moral exceptions. We demonstrate this approach by developing a model that simulates human moral reasoning using a large language model trained on a dataset of human moral judgments. Our results show that the model provides a reasonable account of human moral reasoning and outperforms baseline models in predicting moral exceptions.
A complete intersection domain over a field of prime characteristic $p$ is approximated by toric rings.

This research explores key aspects of the relativistic Dirac equation in a two-dimensional space by examining critical elements that are often overlooked in derivative models like the Schr\"odinger equation and the Klein-Gordon equation. Specifically, it demonstrates that even when the potential is constant, the solution displays non-trivial oscillatory behavior across all space, a phenomenon not seen in non-relativistic models. Notably, this oscillatory behavior is linked to the relativistic nature of the system and is crucial for a precise prediction of the relativistic energy's linear increase with velocity. Furthermore, the study highlights the intricate relationship between the particle's mass, charge, and the coupling constant within the Dirac equation.

This research explores two key issues in autonomous transportation: cooperative adaptive cruise control (CAC) and vehicle platooning. By employing a limited look-ahead model (MPC), this study aims to investigate the impact of communication delays within a network of vehicles on both CAC and platooning. A new approach to modeling and quantifying communication delays is introduced, which is then applied to a scenario involving multiple vehicles. The proposed method takes into account the time it takes for messages to be transmitted, processed, and received, as well as the fact that communication failures can occur at any point. Simulation results demonstrate that using MPC can effectively mitigate the negative consequences of communication failures, particularly when vehicles are closely spaced and the number of vehicles in the network is high.

This study assesses Twitter users' trustworthiness by gauging their credibility based on their followers-to-following ratio and recent activity pattern. A credibility metric is developed to measure the trustworthiness of users with a substantial follower count. Furthermore, we propose a classification system to evaluate the trustworthiness of users with a large following count. Our approach classifies users into four reliability categories: trusted, questionable, blocked, and unknown. We use real-world data from Twitter to demonstrate that our method effectively distinguishes reputable from untrustworthy users with high prediction accuracy for users with a large follower count.

In the future V2X network, on-demand urgent services are crucial and can be significantly enhanced by the on-demand slicing concept. To tackle the complex service request management, especially under high traffic conditions, this paper introduces $\pi$-ROAD - a novel framework utilizing machine learning techniques to provide on-demand services efficiently. Initially, the framework employs data-driven learning to create accurate models of vehicle services and network characteristics. Next, the learned models are combined into a probabilistic neural network that predicts on-demand service paths with high accuracy. Furthermore, the framework includes an on-demand slice creation mechanism that optimizes resource utilization and service latency. Finally, the framework enables on-demand service adaptation by selecting the most suitable service paths based on changing network conditions and resource availability. Extensive simulations demonstrate that $\pi$-ROAD effectively reduces on-demand service latency by 27% and improves network slice success rate by 11%, outperforming traditional V2X slicing schemes.

Factories are shifting to a human-robot collaboration model where humans work alongside robots that assume various roles, either performing tasks alongside robots or guiding the robots in shared workspaces. This new setup necessitates the development of a tactile display system for humans to effectively interact with robots. This research project, CoHaptics, aims to create a wearable tactile display for human-robot collaboration in factories where humans and robots interact and share tasks. The proposed wearable tactile display is designed to be simple, adaptable, and discreet, providing tactile feedback to humans through tactile elements on their forearms. The primary objective is to increase human safety by developing an intuitive and natural human-robot collaboration system. The project involves the development of a wearable tactile display for human-robot interaction and collaboration, with prototypes created for testing purposes. The project's outcomes will be shared at international conferences for potential adoption in factory settings.

As self-driving vehicles move towards practical application, it's crucial for the development of standards and shared communication language between key stakeholders to begin as soon as possible. To ensure that the complex needs of urban settings are taken into consideration, SAE Level 5 vehicles need to be designed not only for individual safety but also for reliable operation in diverse environments. A proposed standard for encoding autonomy-related data and urban environment characteristics could significantly contribute to the widespread adoption of self-driving vehicles.

This research explores the fundamental limits of an online caching model known as the two-armed cache, where each item in a class is assigned a unique weight and the task is to select the item with the maximum weight from a fixed-size subset each time. A key factor influencing the selection is the weight of the chosen item and the information from a feature vector provided for each item. To make a selection at each time step, the method first uses a linear separator to transform the feature vector into advice that guides the choice, and then the item with the maximum weight, transformed similarly, is picked. A lower bound is established that shows the minimum achievable competitive ratio of this model is $\Omega(\sqrt{n} / \log n)$, where n denotes the size of the subset. This is the first time an lower bound has been found that doesn't rely on the feature dimension. A new method is developed that uses a specific type of feature vector, derived from a neural network trained to distinguish between well-chosen and poorly chosen items from the same class, and achieves a competitive ratio of $O(\sqrt{n} / \log n)$. This method also features a small feature dimension and relies on only $O(\log n)$ neural network parameters.

Automating the segmentation of medical images has become a critical requirement for efficient clinical, statistical, and research processes. Despite significant advancements in segmentation techniques, existing approaches often struggle with real-time performance, particularly for large-scale medical images. In response to this need, a novel method called the Trilateral Focus Network (TFN) has been developed to provide accurate and fast medical image segmentation. This method utilizes a combination of multi-scale dilated convolutions, multi-scale attention modules, and multi-scale dilated group convolutions to focus on key features and improve the accuracy and efficiency of the segmentation process. By leveraging the capabilities of deep learning, TFN enables seamless end-to-end training and automatic learning of critical parameters. Through experiments on large-scale medical images, TFN has demonstrated its ability to achieve state-of-the-art segmentation performance while significantly improving processing speed.

Eleven-dimensional supergravity is described through linearized supergeometry, incorporating four local supersymmetries whose parameter transformations depend on dependent variables introduced by Witten. These dependent variables, however, do not satisfy all the background field equations of supersymmetry, and the commutator of the supersymmetry transformations does so either. This commutator is expressed in terms of an additional differential operator that acts on the dependent variables, and the used gauge choice ensures the operator's vanishing.

Machine learning relies heavily on data quality, making it challenging to identify poor training results due to poor data and its impact on subsequent processes. 
Consequently, it's essential to recognize unsatisfactory predictions in real-time and adjust the learning process accordingly. 
This study introduces an adaptable method to refine the accuracy of predictions generated by Gradient Boosting Decision Trees in a sequential environment. 
The core idea revolves around leveraging the training process to identify subspaces where predictions diverge from the expected outcome and use this information to inform the model, thereby minimizing the impact of poor predictions on its performance. 
Experiments on four diverse datasets across various domains demonstrate the proposed approach's effectiveness in addressing data-related inaccuracies without requiring extra computational resources.

In the study of QHE, the standard transformation for calculating the energy level $E_{\rm N}$ is based on the operator $e^{i\phi\hat{\mathbf{k}}_n\cdot\hat{\mathbf{r}}_n}$. However, this approach is impractical due to the need to solve a high-order differential equation for the Nth power of the momentum. Instead, we propose an alternative method for computing the Nth Landau level using a modified Hamiltonian: $\hat{\mathbf{H}}_{\rm N} = \hat{\mathbf{H}_0} + \hat{\mathbf{H}_N}$. Here, the unitary operator $e^{i\hat{\mathbf{H}}_N} $ transforms the system into the Nth Landau level, and we find that the eigenstates of $\hat{\mathbf{H}}_N$ are the Nth Landau level states. This approach eliminates the need to solve a high-order differential equation and instead requires solving a first-order differential equation for the Nth power of the operator. We term this method the qubit transformation for qubits in the context of QHE.

Recent breakthroughs in automatic encoding of language models have been made possible through the application of autoencoding denoising objectives, leading to state-of-the-art results across various natural language processing tasks. Nevertheless, training large-scale language models using autoencoding denoising objectives poses a significant challenge due to the computational and memory-intensive nature of the problem. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces an alternative autoencoding denoising objective known as the Model-generated signal Enhanced Transformer objective (METRO). This novel objective leverages a signal generation approach to create enhanced denoising effects within transformer models, thereby enhancing their capacity to learn more robust feature representations. Furthermore, METRO can be efficiently implemented using a multi-task learning framework, enabling the simultaneous training of multiple sub-tasks using a single model. Experimental evaluations conducted on the WikiText-103 and Enwik8 benchmarks have demonstrated METRO's superiority over existing autoencoding denoising objectives, showcasing its potential to train large-scale transformer models with enhanced performance.

Inferring the global network link between various nodes is crucial in understanding many real-world and simulated systems with interconnected components. In a randomly connected spin system with two possible states, we investigate the feasibility of determining the complete network topology using minimum measurements of neighboring node correlations. This research is motivated by the need to infer complex network structure, particularly in cases where complete topological information is unavailable due to constraints. In such systems, it is often more cost-effective to acquire local node information, and our study explores the effectiveness of a measurement-based approach to infer the global network structure. In the case of a fully interconnected system, we find that a limited number of measurements (proportional to the system size) are sufficient to achieve accurate inference with high probability, and the same holds true for a random power-law network with varying node degrees.

Initial descriptions of visualizations play a crucial role in facilitating understanding between creators and stakeholders by conveying the essence of the data, analysis, or transformation presented in a visual. This study examined the role of initial descriptions in the context of IEEE InfoVis 2017, where participants generated descriptions for 30 visualizations, resulting in 489 crowdsourced descriptions. We analyzed these descriptions, identified patterns, and extracted quotes, concluding that the most effective descriptions employ specific strategies, including (i) linking the visualization to a relevant concept or process, (ii) specifying the data transformation, and (iii) providing a context for comparison. These strategies enable stakeholders to rapidly comprehend the visualization's purpose.

In situations where data is uncertain, it's essential to consider the uncertainty in model parameters in order to make informed decisions and set targets for fairness and equity. We analyze a specific scenario where the outcome of a decision-maker's action is uncertain, and develop a framework to evaluate strategies based on their performance under varying conditions. Our research provides tools for comparing and assessing counterfactual strategies, which aim to achieve specific goals under uncertainty, and demonstrates the practical applications of these strategies in real-world scenarios.

Urban Sound Tagging's algorithmic progress has been hindered by the lack of accessible, openly-distributed data. Public datasets, such as Urban Sound Tagging's own dataset, are frequently limited in size and often contaminated with labeling errors. In an effort to promote progress in Urban Sound Tagging, the Urban Sound Tagging v1 dataset has been widely used, yet its distinct distribution can greatly skew comparison results for machine learning algorithms. To provide a more equitable platform for comparing algorithms, we recommend using a version of the Urban Sound Tagging v1 dataset with corrected labels and sound samples, thereby ensuring a fair comparison of machine learning models' performance.

We explore the supersymmetric AdS4 black holes that arise in specific gauged supergravity theories with matter included. These theories, which have N=3 and N=4 supersymmetry, exhibit scalar-tensor and scalar-floatable gauged supergravities respectively. We identify the most general form of the gauged superalgebras in these theories, which includes a U(1) R-symmetry. We then determine the supersymmetric solutions in each of these gauge groups and identify the specific AdS4 black hole vacua that preserve one supersymmetry. These vacuities are found to be distinct from those that arise in pure gauged supergravies, which suggests that incorporating matter could lead to a richer landscape of possible vacuities.

This paper introduces Cain, a novel approach for automatically generating code to optimize the processing of focal-plane sensors in cameras. By utilizing machine learning, Cain can translate a high-level specification into optimized code for executing convolutional kernels on the vast array of diverse sensor processors found in various devices. By automatically adapting to the specific architecture of the sensor processor, as well as the specific requirements of the input data, Cain offers significant performance benefits. In contrast to existing manual optimization methods that are time-consuming and error-prone, Cain enables seamless integration of the full range of available convolutional kernels on camera sensors. By doing so, it can significantly reduce the complexity of camera systems and enable new applications, such as camera arrays and real-time video processing. In our evaluation, Cain successfully achieved an average performance boost of 3.2x over the optimized code, while also completing the optimization process in less than 30 seconds for 90% of the tested sensor processors.

We investigate the D-term dynamics of type IIB supergravity in a background with non-linear sigma model terms that incorporate a general metric and B-field. Focusing on configurations with spontaneously broken U(1)R-symmetry, we derive an appropriate theta-term through an appropriate Weyl transformation, effectively generalising the previously established Kähler B-field used in N=1 backgrounds to these new configurations. This approach is illustrated by applying the analysis to the Abelian (A0)2-field strength of a D3-brane in a background with a metric and B-field, and by computing the theta-term in a D3-brane solitonic sector of AdS5 x S5.

In high-stakes fields like medicine and finance, it's crucial to make informed decisions to achieve desired outcomes, but this process is often hindered by uncertainty and risk. To address this, we can utilize reinforcement learning to identify decision strategies that minimize uncertainty and unwanted outcomes in situations with limited data. To tackle this complex problem, we've developed a new approach called ROSE, which uses regret optimization to identify the best possible strategies. By analyzing sequences of actions and outcomes, we can create a decision framework that balances the need to gather information with the goal of achieving the desired outcome, all while efficiently using computational resources. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we've tested it in a simulated environment and found it to outperform existing algorithms in achieving the desired outcome with the fewest possible uncertainties.

Aristotle's logical system in his "Prior Analytics" presents a challenge due to its complex and non-standard structure, which has led most interpreters to rephrase it in modern notation for the sake of simplicity. This approach results in losing the original connection to the broader Aristotelian logical system. This paper proposes an innovative method to re-express the logical system in modal syllogistic notation while maintaining a clear connection to the other parts of Aristotelian logic. This new framework demonstrates its feasibility by successfully proving the equivalent of Modus Ponens and Modus Tollens within the system's own logic.

Quantum causality detection methods have garnered significant attention in the
realm of quantum information research. However, the existing implementation of
this causality detection involves a complex process that can be exploited to
mount a powerful attack. Our investigation delves into the feasibility of this
attack and examines potential strategies to counter it.

In high-efficiency video coding (HEVC) and video coding level 5 (VVC), assigning an optimal bit allocation to each video frame is essential for achieving optimal compression results. This study proposes a novel dual-critic reinforcement learning framework that addresses frame-level bit allocation, integrating a binary quantization module and a multi-step transition mechanism to enhance the learning efficiency and bit allocation accuracy. The experimental outcomes reveal that our proposed method outperforms VTM 13 and other baseline solutions, demonstrating a bit savings ratio of 0.5% and 1.2% in comparison to VTM 5 and VTM 1 respectively, with a significantly reduced training time of 25.6% compared to VTM 1. Furthermore, our framework is highly scalable, with the ability to be extended to more complex scenarios such as 3D transition, by integrating additional critic networks.

The formation of stars and their companion planets is associated with the gradual cooling of a disk of material surrounding the developing star. As the disk cools, the balance of chemical components changes, leading to a significant increase in the amount of graphite relative to other carbon-based particles. A team of researchers has created a new model that accounts for the behavior of carbon-based particles within the disk, simulating various scenarios to understand how different components interact and how the rate of carbon deposition changes under different conditions. They found that a combination of factors, including the reduction of larger graphite particles and the lack of smaller graphite particles, leads to a significant decrease in the rate of carbon deposition. This decrease in the rate of carbonization is caused by a process in which the smaller graphite particles are consumed by the destruction of larger graphite particles, which in turn causes a decrease in the number of smaller graphite particles, leading to a decrease in the rate of carbonization. This model was able to accurately simulate the observed cooling of the disk and the resulting increase in the amount of graphite relative to other carbon-based particles.

In this work, we propose an approach to select cutting planes for the branch and bound optimization method, drawing from the concept of imitation learning. Our model, called the Imitation Cutting Plane Selector (ICPS), learns to select cutting planes by replicating the behavior of a seasoned solver, allowing for improved solution times on complex problem sets. Furthermore, we investigate the practical application of deep learning in solving large-scale mixed-integer linear programs, demonstrating that selecting cutting planes can serve as a crucial intermediate step.

In this study, we have investigated the superconducting properties of Mo$_{0.9}$Ir$_{0.1}$Te$_{2}$, a compound that maintains nonmagnetic, topological properties, yet exhibits disrupted inversion symmetry. Our findings reveal a superconducting phase at 2.0(1) Kelvin, which is significantly lower than the previously observed critical temperature of 7.2(1) Kelvin in the undoped compound. Our analysis of the superconducting state indicates that it is a type-II superconductor and that the lower transition temperature can be attributed to pair breaking caused by magnetic impurities. Additionally, we have determined the upper critical magnetic field and found that it is comparable to the previously observed upper critical field in the undoped compound.

Effective bug tracking is heavily dependent on the accuracy of bug labels, which is often hindered by inconsistent or incorrect tagging practices within development teams. To address this challenge, an auto-tagging system has been created that streamlines the bug tracking process by utilizing machine learning techniques to automate the assignment of accurate labels to bug reports from various software development projects. Upon evaluating our system with existing tools, our proposed model demonstrated superior performance across multiple metrics, including accuracy, precision, and recall.

We investigate the impact of anisotropy and relativity on the phase transitions in graphene-like materials. We found that the anisotropy distorts the phase diagram, driving the line of second-order transitions into a three-dimensional structure, characterized by a single winding number determined by anisotropy. As relativity increases, this line disappears, replaced by two separate lines representing the transitions in the anisotropic and isotropic phases. We determined the critical exponents for each line and the adjacent critical points, and found that the transitions in the anisotropic phase are of first order, while those in the isotropic phase are of second order. We also discovered that the anisotropic phase exhibits a distinct critical point, which is a line of zero dimension, and that the transitions between the anisotropic and isotropic phases are of first order.

In many fields, like biology and medicine, the need for human annotation is often impractically high due to the scarcity of experts available for labeling. This has led to significant costs and delays in the application of NLP. In response, we examine a new framework for low-resource named entity recognition that leverages a dynamic interplay between multiple machine learning models and provides accurate results without relying on extensive annotation. By using an unsupervised learning approach, we train a machine learning model, called the "teacher," by optimizing its architecture through various combinations of ensemble learning and knowledge transfer. This teacher model is then used to train a group of student models, each of which is specifically tailored to a particular subset of the data. We also develop an innovative method to efficiently select relevant data chunks and corresponding weights for each student, ensuring optimal performance. In our experiments, we demonstrate that our adaptive teacher learning approach, paired with our fine-grained ensemble and weight optimization techniques, produces superior results compared to existing methods.

Every year, 1.2 billion people engage in tourism, resulting in a vast and diverse stream of travel-related social media data. This expansive dataset contains valuable information about tourists' travel experiences, despite being embedded within a noisy and fragmented text environment. To extract insights from this data, researchers can utilize natural language processing techniques to identify relevant patterns. This paper presents a method for automatically categorizing and refining noisy social media data to create a resource for researchers studying tourism, demonstrating its effectiveness with a case study involving London tourism.

A new model, the data-driven model, has been developed to generate microstructure images that are accurate and computationally efficient for simulating composite materials with intricate internal structures. This model uses a type of neural network called a generative adversarial network to produce high-quality microstructure images that match those found in real-world materials. By utilizing this model, researchers can create highly realistic simulations of composite materials that are indistinguishable from those generated from actual experiments. The data-driven model has been successfully applied to predict the mechanical properties of composite materials with various loadings and display a notable improvement in their accuracy.

Young stars with gas disks that are less than 5 million years old are anticipated to have their companion stars at a distance greater than 10 astronomical units.  However, a star known as CI Tau has a gas disk that is comprised of a large ring, measuring 50 astronomical units in size.  Despite this, imaging data collected around CI Tau reveals the presence of a companion star at a distance of 8 astronomical units from the star.  This companion star is thought to be a source of gravitational perturbations within the CI Tau gas disk.  Notably, a large ring, measuring 50 astronomical units in size is the largest known gas disk in the T Tauri population.  This study's imaging data collected at the 8 meter Gemini North telescope, in the infrared spectrum, is the first to achieve an imaging depth of 10 magnitudes at the 5 million year mark. The development of a new type of space station with a unique orbit is being explored. The proposed space station will have a special pattern in its design, resulting from the orbit it follows around the Earth. The station's path will be circular at a constant altitude, but its living areas will experience varying levels of rotation due to the way it orbits, causing these regions to be tilted at an angle. The unique orbit is intended to simulate a gravity environment similar to that on the International Space Station but with an added feature of an extra g-force component. The advantages of this special orbit are that it allows for the simulation of a g-force without the need for additional engines and provides a means of adjusting the level of simulated gravity by adjusting the rate of rotation, all without affecting the balance of thrust. The research into this type of orbit is ongoing, with a focus on determining the feasibility of implementing such a unique orbit and the specific design requirements for the system. The development of a new type of space station with a unique orbit is an innovative step towards creating a more realistic simulation of gravity in a low-gravity environment, with potential implications for the design of future space research stations.

This study focuses on the most effective methods for establishing the most precise Sobolev-type inequalities for non-local equations on a compact surface. The research involves investigating the optimal inequality related to the $LP$ operator and developing analytical tools such as the Fourier expansion of eigenfunctions on manifolds. The analysis also includes finding the most critical eigenvalue and eigenfunction for a specific optimization problem, as well as determining the optimal inequality for a particular Sobolev functional. The findings provide new insights on the impact of spatial curvature on the optimal inequality, revealing that high positive curvature leads to optimal inequality degradation.

A novel approach for tracking multiple targets through motion sensors involves 
utilizing a path-based rather than track-based methodology. This novel method 
involves two main steps: first, determining the most probable path given known 
sensor data; and second, using this path to generate a likelihood distribution 
for the targets' possible locations given the sensor data. This new method is 
tested and its effectiveness demonstrated using a real-world dataset.

This study examines the stability assessment of multi-feed grid-connected converter systems using impedance and admittance matrices, with a focus on stability evaluation. To analyze stability, small-signal perturbations are analyzed in the frequency domain to derive the system's closed-loop transfer function. This transfer function is then determined from the admittance matrix of the system, taking into account the external grid impedance. Furthermore, sensitivity analysis is performed to determine the impact of admittance matrix elements on stability. This analysis is complemented by a comparison of impedance and admittance admittance matrix models, as well as the use of small-signal modulation depth to predict stability.

The reliability of online signature authentication largely hinges on the stability of digital signature templates. This paper delves into the consistency of online signature templates from both a theoretical and practical perspective. Initially, we examine uniqueness, a fundamental characteristic of online signature templates, which involves determining the likelihood of mistakenly linking an unknown signature to an existing identity. Subsequently, we investigate the diversity of online signature templates, represented by the Hamming distance between individuals' signature patterns. Ultimately, we assess the stability of online signature templates through repeated signature acquisition and analyze the computational demands associated with these measurements.
This text presents two geometric interpretations of the Hardy sum $\sum_{j=0}^{n}\left|\frac{1}{2^{j+1/2}}-\frac{1}{2^{j+3/4}+x^{1/4}}\right|$, one utilizing a circle and the other a sphere.

This research introduces a new method for understanding the complex interplay between factors like a car's engine and driving conditions when operating a system with multiple interconnected processes. To capture these interactions, we assign each process an evolving contextual state that influences its behavior. We then analyze the system's dynamics using a mathematical framework, which enables us to identify patterns in the interactions between contextual states across different processes. Furthermore, we propose a specific system architecture that utilizes inter-process communication to replicate the observed patterns in real-world scenarios.

This study introduces an innovative method for estimating three-dimensional human motion from video. By incorporating a hierarchical attention mechanism into our model, we enable it to prioritize and focus on the most relevant depth sequences for more accurate pose predictions. Additionally, we employ dilated convolutional layers to process video sequences at varied frame rates without frame rate normalization. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through its outperformance in experiments on the Human3.6M dataset, where it achieved superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed model's video-based generalization capabilities are also explored, showcasing its ability to accurately estimate poses from videos with missing frames.

A technique for gauging the intensity of X-rays emanating from the Earth-Sun direction is presented, making use of occultation data obtained by the AstroSat CZTI detector. With 16 units covering a 3.2-deg field of view, the detector monitors the all-sky X-ray distribution. A method to calculate X-ray flux from the AstroSat orbit from a single occultation is developed, allowing for a direct assessment of the solar X-ray flux as well as that of the bright Earth surface regions. This technique can be applied to other space-based X-ray detectors that have sufficient directional sensitivity, thus opening up possibilities for real-time, global X-ray mapping.

The underpinnings of blockchain's operational framework are rooted in the
reliance on unalterable ledger entries, unbreakable cryptographic methods,
and decentralized network operations, resulting in a considerable increase in
computational complexity relative to traditional databases. This phenomenon is
exemplified by a comparison between Bitcoin's validation process and that of
Amazon Simple Storage, highlighting the magnitude of this growth from order
$O(n)$ to $O(n^4)$, depending on block size. This paper undertakes an in-depth
examination of the efficiency of consensus protocols, specifically focusing on
the most widely adopted consensus algorithm BFT, through theoretical modeling and
analysis. This investigation aims to elucidate the inherent trade-offs between
the scalability of blockchain networks, the robustness of their security, and
their operational efficiency.

In our study, we explore the mass spectra of doubly heavy tetraquarks ($[QQ\bar{Q}\bar{Q}$]) by employing a non-relativistic Hamiltonian model with an enhanced chromomagnetic interaction. This model reveals that the states $[cc\bar{q}\bar{q}$] and $[bb\bar{q}\bar{q}$] can be categorized into two types based on their spin configurations: $S=0$ and $S=1$. Utilizing the values of tetraquark masses derived from the $S=0$ and $S=1$ configurations, we observe that the ground states of $D_{0}^{*}(2383)$ and $B_{0}^{*}(18.94)$ align closely with the observed masses of $D_{0}^{*}(2800)^{+}$ and $B_{0}^{*}(20.8)$, respectively. Furthermore, we predict that the $S=1$ states of $cc\bar{q}\bar{q}$ and $bb\bar{q}\bar{q}$ will be the lowest-lying excited states of $S=0$ configurations.

The Higgs vacuum instability issue might hold the key to explaining the electroweak gauge hierarchy. By treating the top-quark mass as a free parameter and incorporating the effect of a large number of light fermions, it is possible to balance the vacuum energy of the electroweak and the Planck scales, as predicted by the effective field theory. The required range for the top-quark mass is relatively narrow, extending from approximately 0.75 TeV to about 1.2 TeV, with the lower boundary being subject to certain boundary conditions. This solution also aligns with the theoretical limitations of fine-tuning in the context of the polynomial effective field theory.

This note investigates the $p$-Talagrand and the $q$-Logarithmic Sobolev inequalities within the framework of Carnot groups and left-invariant stencils. The analysis yields specific outcome for $p=2$ and $q=2$ with a constant determined by formula (2.1). The established inequalities are a consequence of the $L^2$-Poincare inequality, demonstrating their interdependence.

This work explores the minimum variance estimation of the Bregman divergence. It presents a new class of estimators, developed through a transformation of a fixed, minimax estimator using a monotone increasing differentiable function. It's proven that, under certain regular conditions, the Bregman divergence of the proposed estimator and the observation vector reaches its minimum with respect to the parameter, a property that remains valid for large sample sizes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, under a certain regularity condition, the proposed estimator achieves the minimum Bregman divergence with respect to the mean parameter in the context of exponential families. Finally, a simulation study and a real-data application to the Gaussian distribution reveals that the proposed estimator consistently outperforms other existing estimators in terms of Bregman divergence.

We introduce wildNeRF, a novel neural rendering technique, designed to generate high-quality images of dynamic scenes from a single, partially-sparse monocular camera setup, encompassing scenes unseen during training. Our approach enables the creation of novel views and of unseen dynamic scenes within the entire 4π dynamics sphere. To our knowledge, this is the first method capable of capturing an entire dynamic 4π dynamics sphere from a single, partially-sparse monocular camera dataset, encompassing scenes unseen during training. wildNeRF achieves this through a two-stage process. Initially, it utilizes a sparse, partially-sparse dataset to derive a temporal motion representation, capturing essential information about dynamic objects within the 4π dynamics sphere. Next, it employs this acquired motion representation to train a NeRF model, incorporating the sequence-specific features into its neural radiance field. Our approach is validated through a series of experiments, encompassing both synthetic and real-world datasets, yielding comparable results to existing methods.

Researchers have developed a method to study a statistical feature of quantum graphs with no need for the pre-existing knowledge of quantum mechanics, specifically the semiclassical principle. This technique, which relies on periodic orbits, has been successfully applied to several examples, where it demonstrated a consistent outcome in alignment with the semiclassical theory. This paper aims to present additional cases, where the periodic orbit method is used to calculate a statistical statistic in a more general framework without relying on the semiclassical principle. This is made possible by considering the statistics of link and junction points within the graph. Periodic topological invariants can be used to determine the independent paths that contribute to the statistics, and in the case of a graph with multiple topological uniques, it is necessary to select a subset of the periodic orbits to match the number of invariants. This method is applied to two examples, where it shows a consistent outcome in relation to the semiclassical theory.

A novel approach has been developed for estimating the period intervals of periodic variable stars. The method is founded on the cluster analysis of period data using the K-means algorithm. It categorizes periods into distinct groups and calculates the centroid for each cluster. The intervals are then defined by the upper and lower limits of the clusters, and the gaps between them are determined by the distances between adjacent centroids. The method's performance is evaluated using the American Association of Variable Star Experts' period distribution for periodic variable stars. The results show that this method provides a more accurate and efficient way to establish these intervals compared to existing methods, and the methodology is also applied to the PAVO dataset on Long Period Variable stars.

The Negative Imaginary (NI) framework offers a groundbreaking approach to distributed, coordinated control of linear, interconnected systems. By modeling each of the system's components as NI plants, the framework simplifies the design of the overall interconnection as an equivalent system with a stable structure. This concept has been leveraged to develop an algorithm for finding nearly optimal controllers for complex systems, as well as for identifying the system interactions that correspond to specified NI structures. We introduce a novel method for approximating NI structures with a given accuracy, based on a sequence of increasingly accurate representations of the system's dynamics. This method is then applied to two problems: designing controllers for systems with a known NI structure, as well as identifying such structures in systems with linear interactions. We demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our approach through a series of numerical examples.

Automatic Speech Recognition models trained on large-scale corpora are extremely
resource-intensive and typically exhibit the "forgetting problem" when adapting to new
tasks. To mitigate this challenge, pre-trained models with large corpora can be
fine-tuned through a process called warm-starting. However, this approach falls short when
a model is exposed to unfamiliar domains such as varying accents or languages, necessitating
the incorporation of novel strategies. Continual learning, a novel paradigm, aims to enhance
the stability of Automatic Speech Recognition models by iteratively updating them with a steady
flow of new data without overwriting previous knowledge. A proposed framework, Incremental
Fine-tuning, empowers the model to evolve in harmony with new data, fostering a balanced
growth of knowledge acquisition and retention.

Code-switching among languages is a widespread phenomenon observed in everyday conversations and social media interactions. This intricate language phenomenon has garnered research in both NLP and SLA contexts. A sentiment analysis task was undertaken within SemEval-2020, with a focus on code-switching tweets. This paper details our participation in this challenge, with a deep-learning classifier being our primary approach. Code-switching between English and Spanish was specifically examined. Notably, our proposed classifier achieved a 67% micro-averaged F1-score, while also exploring the influence of code-mixing on sentiment analysis.

A theoretical model is proposed for the origin of light neutrino masses and the high-energy density of cosmic lepton and dark-matter particles in the universe.  The model's seesaw mechanism, which involves the conversion of supersymmetric superpartners of the Higgs boson into the light neutrinos, is a complex process that is confirmed to be feasible at low energies.  The model's radiative seesaw mechanism, which involves the conversion of supersymmetric superpartners of the Higgs boson into the light neutrinos, is a process that is mediated by a specific type of particle that is a mixture of the light neutrinos and the supersymmetric superpartners of the Higgs boson.  The model's low-energy density of cosmic lepton particles in the universe can be explained by a specific type of particle decay process, which involves the decay of supersymmetric superpartners of the Higgs boson into the light neutrinos and the supersymmetric superpartners of the light neutrinos.  The model's low-energy density of cosmic dark-matter particles in the universe can be explained by a specific type of particle decay process, which involves the decay of supersymmetric superpartners of the Higgs boson into the light neutrinos and the supersymmetric superpartners of the light neutrinos.  The model's predictions for the origin of cosmic lepton and dark-matter particles in the universe are consistent with the current most accurate measurements of their properties. In recent years, user response prediction has become a significant focus area within large-scale text communication platforms. Accurate forecasting the nature of user responses (such as likes, replies, etc) greatly enhances the user experience by enabling the system to suggest timely and relevant content. Most existing methods rely heavily on traditional machine learning techniques, utilizing advanced natural language processing and information retrieval methods. However, recent advancements in deep learning have shown considerable promise in this domain. Our research involves developing an innovative neural network model specifically designed to forecast user responses. This proposed model incorporates items-based recommendations and achieves a notable improvement in predictive accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, yielding improvements of up to 2.5% in F1-Score.

Cell-free networks utilizing intelligent reflecting surfaces are gaining attention for mitigating interference and enhancing energy efficiency. However, the phase shift errors due to inaccurate channel estimation can cause signal degradation at the receiver end. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a robust joint design of BSs and IRSs, focusing on minimizing the channel estimation error in cell-free networks. By leveraging long short-term signal-aided channel estimation, the phase shift factor is designed as a robust parameter to counteract the channel estimation error, while BSs' beamforming vectors are optimized to maximize the system's energy efficiency. The problem is formulated into an alternating optimization framework, where each variable is optimized sequentially. The optimization problem is then solved using the OMP algorithm, and a low complexity algorithm is proposed to update the BSs' beamforming vectors. The simulation results demonstrate that the proposed robust joint design significantly outperforms existing schemes in terms of energy efficiency, with the maximum achievable values of 0.55, 0.5, and 0.46 dB at 5, 10, and 20 mobile stations, respectively.

Deep learning based approaches have been gaining traction in branch prediction. However, traditional methods focus on static branches, leaving deep learning based dynamic branch prediction struggling to meet industry standards. Previous works have shown some promise but were plagued by significant performance degradation and memory constraints. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of deep learning based dynamic branch prediction techniques, exploring their design aspects and discussing their various shortcomings. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes dynamic branch instruction data to improve prediction accuracy and proposes a method to minimize memory overhead.

Imitation learning, a key framework in computer vision research, has gained significant attention in robotics due to its potential to bypass costly teaching processes. This study proposes an imitation-driven solution to automatic camera control, where a deep neural network learns to replicate human camera operations by observing control sequences from a tracker. A novel imitation framework is developed, combining a convolutional neural network with a classification algorithm, and its efficacy is demonstrated through a series of experiments with a robotic platform, showcasing improved performance and reduced runtime. Furthermore, the proposed approach exhibits high generalization capabilities, achieving comparable results with leading methods even in unseen scenarios.

The equation we're interested in has an integer value of n that is greater than or equal equivalent to 3, and it has an integer value of k that is greater than or equal to -2. We also define a variable, h, that encompasses values less than 1 and greater than -1, and we consider an SO(3) rotation that has an integer value of n or less. We then introduce a parameter, theta, that encompasses values less than pi/2, and we consider an SO(2) rotation that has an integer value of n or less. The EIT-based method of quantum state transfer has been extended to enable its application in diverse environments. We have developed a straightforward approach to determine the optimal length required for resonant photon entanglement via EIT-based state transfer, which can be easily adapted for use in either loss or gain situations. Furthermore, we found that the proposed method remains effective against interference caused by Raman scattering. This advancement paves the way for implementing quantum applications in various settings, such as fiber communications and biological sensing, where the use of fixed power levels or weak coupling is unavoidable.

Within the context of light-cone QCD sum rules, recent studies have employed light vector mesons to couple with ground and excited scalar and pseudoscalar mesons containing charm and bottom flavors. The study has yielded key outcomes, including the determination of coupling constants resistant to Poincaré symmetry breaking, which hold considerable significance for assessing hadronic light-front distributions. Notably, the research reveals that the coupling strength for bottom mesons exceeds its charm counterpart, an observation consistent with theoretical expectations based on heavy quark symmetry.

The discovery of neutrino oscillations has confirmed that neutrinos have masses and mass splittings, but the precise mass differences and the mixing angles between neutrino states are still unknown. This missing information is crucial for understanding various aspects of neutrino behavior and would be essential for resolving several fundamental issues, including what triggers the matter-antimatter asymmetry in the Universe, what governs flavor mixing, and what causes the breaking of lepton flavor number. This paper offers an overview of the ongoing neutrino experiments and outlines the capabilities of upcoming neutrino studies that are anticipated to provide more detailed insights into several key aspects of neutrinos, including mass hierarchy, major mixing angles, and other properties, such as charged lepton flavor violation, dark matter, and more.

A key concept in causal inference is to determine the causal effect of a single variable while disregarding all others.  A straightforward yet limited method is simply conducting a solitary regression analysis.  However, a more effective strategy is to utilize a weighted least squares estimator that assigns a zero weight to confounding variables.  Although the specific choice of weightings has not been thoroughly explored, particularly in scenarios involving multiple variables, weightings for the singular variable of interest or confounders have been examined.  This paper investigates the selection of weights that facilitate causal inference when dealing with multiple variables.  It reveals that weights enabling causal identification must assign zero weight to confounding variables and a positive weight to the variable of interest.  Furthermore, a particular set of weights allows the weighted least squares estimator to converge on the causal parameter of interest.  These findings are illustrated through an example.

This paper introduces a novel control approach for large-scale power electronic devices connected to a power grid. The proposed method leverages the dynamic characteristics of the power system using wide-area measurement units and transmission system monitoring to efficiently damp low-frequency oscillations in the system. By achieving a near-optimal balance between energy consumption and control signals, this approach requires only basic voltage and current measurements from system devices. The effectiveness of the method is evaluated through a comprehensive analysis of the IEEE 68-bus system, facilitating the exploration of key factors such as the impact of energy compensation, control signals, and device location on the system's performance.

The behavior of two atoms interacting with a common reservoir, particularly when one of the atoms is far away from the other, has been widely studied in the past. In this study, we examine the effects of this distance on the collective emission of two identical atoms when they're both near the reservoir. The findings reveal that, as the distance between the atoms increases, the overall rate at which they decay together (subradiance) is actually enhanced, particularly in the case of two identical atoms when one of them is alone in the reservoir, compared to having them in close proximity. This enhancement is caused by the reduced interaction between the atoms. Notably, increasing the distance between the atoms also amplifies the overall rate at which they decay together (subradiance) in scenarios where the overall rate approaches zero.

Stable kink solutions to (1+1)-dimensional $\phi^4$ models can be subjected to a specific type of perturbation, yielding a stable internal mode. The perturbation's effect decays exponentially over time, aligning in neither propagation velocity nor the kink's fixed profile. Although this perturbation falls outside conventional invariance categories, kink asymptotic stability is restored.

The J-PARC hadronic fixed target experiments have gathered a substantial dataset on high-energy proton-nucleus collisions, allowing for a thorough investigation of light hadron production. This study leverages the experiment's unique capabilities to explore color transparency with both inclusive and exclusive channels. By analyzing both single-particle and two-particle distributions, researchers can gain insight into the inner workings of high-energy proton-nucleus collisions. This discussion will delve into the experimental implications of color transparency for neutral pion production, specifically focusing on an experiment that combines data from the NEPTUNE and NEUTRINO EXPERIMENT. By analyzing up to 640 GeV pion production, researchers can explore color transparency at unprecedented energies. This study will examine the experimental feasibility of measuring ratios of observables, which can help mitigate systematic uncertainties and provide a clearer understanding of color transparency. By analyzing these ratios, researchers can gain a more accurate picture of nuclear shadowing and phase factors, ultimately shedding light on the internal structure of the proton.

Deep learning models are often compromised by out-of-distribution data, 
causing a decline in their performance. In response, we developed Consistency Training, 
a new method that evaluates a model's robustness by comparing its predictions on 
repeatedly distorted input data. Although successful, the variety of transformations 
used can hinder the optimization process. To address this challenge, we introduce 
a virtual adversarial technique to simulate the data distortions in a discrete form, 
improving the effectiveness of Consistent Training. Experimental results on 
MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and SVHN datasets reveal that our approach surpasses existing 
state-of-the-art methods.

This paper introduces a cutting-edge method for polyp detection in endoscopic videos, focusing on the challenges posed by slow motion and the presence of background motions. To mitigate these issues, the proposed Multi-frame Cooperation (MC) module is introduced, enabling the efficient utilization of multiple video frames to accurately identify polyp motion directions. Additionally, the module transforms spatial features into temporal features, thereby enhancing the robustness of the polyp detection process, as verified through experiments on real data. Evaluations conducted on 115 endoscopic video sequences, divided into two datasets (the SOBAY dataset and a custom dataset), demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed MC module in improving polyp detection accuracy, ultimately leading to an overall detection accuracy of 94.5% and a classification accuracy of 96.5% on the test set.

A novel method has been proposed to address the challenge of estimating animal populations in streams. The new method employs an unequal likelihood sampling framework that uses sequential information to select sampling points along the stream. By incorporating spatial correlation of both animal populations and water circulation into the method, a more accurate sampling design is achieved. This approach allows for more representative animal samples to be collected, thereby enhancing the estimation of animal abundance. Using a hierarchical model, population size and demographic characteristics can be effectively estimated from the obtained data. The proposed method's performance is demonstrated through a simulation study and a practical application in a real-world setting, showcasing its potential for real-world stream population surveys.

Recent discoveries of $^{57}$Zn and $^{56}$Ni through beta-delayed proton emission and mass measurements have provided significant insights into the $rp$ process. Specifically, near the Gamow-Pons peak energy, the abundance of $^{57$Zn in the solar wind is found to be comparable to that of $^{56$Ni. Furthermore, the observation of $^{57$Zn and $^{56$Ni at the Earth's surface suggests that $^{57$Zn undergoes beta minus decay with a half-life of 34.0(4) seconds. These results indicate that $^{57$Zn decays before it can undergo beta minus decay, thereby bypassing the Gamow-Pons peak and significantly affecting the $rp$ process.

We give an explicit, computational finding to a particular instance of the Manin-Mumford prediction. Specifically, for a number field $K$ of degree $n$ over the rational numbers and an imaginary quadratic extension $L$ of $\mathbb{Q}$, we consider the moduli space $\mathcal{A}_{K,L}^1(\mathbb{P}^1,\mathbb{P}^1)$ of isogenies between smooth projective curves over $K$ and $\mathcal{A}_{K,L}^1(\mathbb{P}^1,\mathcal{E})$ where $\mathcal{E}$ is an elliptic curve over $K$. We show that the set of points in $\mathcal{A}_{K,L}^1(\mathbb{P}^1,\mathbb{P}^1)$ that leave $\mathbb{P}^1\backslash K$ invariant has a finite number of translates of $\mathbb{P}^1$ minus $K$. This addresses a long-standing problem first posed by Manin and Mumford in the 1970s.

The association of gamma-ray sources with pulsars is a crucial clue to understanding the creation of gamma-ray emitting pulsars and their connection to high-energy gamma-ray astronomy. The discovery of gamma-ray emission from a few pulsars has been achieved, but many of these pulsars have not been detected at gamma-ray energies. The reasons for this are unclear and could be related to factors such as the age of the pulsar, its distance from Earth, or its surrounding environment. The VERITAS collaboration has carried out extensive observations of 29 pulsars found in the northern sky, focusing on the emission of gamma-ray radiation around these pulsars. The analysis of the data collected during these observations has revealed no signs of gamma-ray radiation above an energy threshold of 0.2 TeV. For the first time, upper limits have been established for the gamma-ray flux emitted by these pulsars in the energy range of 0.1 to 2 TeV, with some of the limits being remarkably low. The upper limits obtained for the gamma-ray flux have been used to calculate the maximum possible luminosity of the pulsars. The maximum possible luminosity of the pulsars has been compared to the observed luminosity of the gamma-ray emitting pulsar PSR J1833-0827, which is consistent with the hypothesis that the observed luminosity is significantly lower than the maximum possible luminosity. The results suggest that the observed luminosity of the gamma-ray emitting pulsar PSR J1833-

This study explores the long-term behavior of a broad set of reaction-diffusion equations with nonlocal boundary conditions across varying domains. Initially, we establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a class of nonlinear equations, covering cases where the boundary conditions are weakly nonlinear and nonlinear Caputo derivatives are employed. Building on this foundation, we demonstrate that for certain anisotropic elliptic operators, our solutions exhibit exponential stability over extended exponential weighted norms. Leveraging this result, we then analyze the long-term behavior of solutions to parabolic equations under the same conditions, and ultimately apply these findings to a broad class of equations, including those defined on fractal-type domains.

A novel machine learning approach has been developed to identify globular clusters and ultra compact dwarfs within galaxy images, allowing for a deeper understanding of their formation and evolution processes to be obtained. The machine learning model was trained using images of these objects and galaxies from the Hubble Space telescope, and it was discovered that a convolutional neural network model performed better compared to a support vector machine, achieving an accuracy rate of 95% or higher. The machine learning model was then used to analyze images of galaxy clusters captured by the Hubble Space telescope, and it was found that it successfully detected a significant number of previously undetected globular clusters and ultra compact dwarfs. The machine learning model was also found to be effective in distinguishing globular clusters and ultra compact dwarfs from background objects, and it was discovered that it can be used to identify and track the evolution of globular clusters and ultra compact dwarfs in real-time.

Recent years have seen a substantial rise in interest for suggesting systems.
Efficient recommender systems are now crucial components of various digital
platforms, enabling users to discover relevant content and pinpoint valuable items.
The vast array of available information necessitates a robust and efficient
mechanism to receive, access, and provide services, which is where suggestion
systems play a vital role. In this paper, we delve into the key elements of
suggesting systems, providing both theoretical and practical perspectives based
on industry expertise.

We investigate the statistical properties of a sample average statistic in a heavy-tailed environment. Theoretical advancements include a new asymptotic framework for the truncated sample average, enabling the derivation of the asymptotic distribution of the difference between the truncated and untruncated versions of the sample average. This framework facilitates the development of an asymptotic hypothesis testing procedure, even in extremely dispersed population scenarios. The proposed method is applied to the testing of mean shifts at the 1% significance level, with results validated through Monte Carlo simulations.

A convolutional neural network (CNN) is a leading approach for classifying motor imagery (MI) signals using electroencephalography (EEG), particularly in the context of human-computer interaction. However, traditional CNNs often rely on filters with a rectangular shape, which can be inefficient due to their fixed size and redundant elements. To address this limitation, a novel CNN with sinc-based filters, called the sinc CNN, has been developed. This approach leverages the properties of the sinc function to create a compact, non-rectangular filter response that enhances the classification performance of MI signals. Experimental results, which utilize the BCI competition IV dataset, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed sinc CNN in MI signal classification, outperforming traditional CNNs and achieving state-of-the-art performance in the field.

We explore the massless tensor field on a $AdS_2$ space that has been further noncommutized. Given that the field's quantum correlation functions are known in commutative space, we use the correspondence rule to calculate them in the noncommutative setting, while also confirming that the solution adheres to the underlying noncommutative field equation.

Kidney transplants often rely on the goodwill of donors, but the process of matching organs to recipients is not always successful. Various experts have suggested using the next available donated organ to fill any gaps, but the ideal strategy for doing so has yet to be established. In our study, we model the process of accepting subsequent donor organs under the assumption that the distribution of remaining waiting times is unknown. Two new methods for accepting organs are proposed, one that operates under random matching of organs to recipients and the other that takes into account the randomness of both matching and patient health. The effectiveness of these strategies is compared to the traditional practice of accepting organs based solely on the unknown distribution of waiting times. The findings suggest that the proposed methods perform better than the current standard in most cases and offer improved outcomes for patients.

This research paper presents and evaluates two novel models that combine features of Hidden Markov Model (HMM) and Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) to accurately forecast time series data. The proposed hybrid models are applied to forecast the monthly average temperature in Kars, Turkey from 1955-2011, utilizing manual segmentation. The models are trained on separate datasets created by HMM to segment the time series data, demonstrating that the hybrid models outperform both HMM and LSTM in terms of mean absolute error.

This research examines some composition properties of the generalized Volterra integral operator, and we demonstrate that for a specific range of parameters α, this operator is a Toeplitz operator with a bounded symbol when acting on weighted Bergman spaces with an exponential weight, effectively giving us a complete list of all bounded symbols associated with the Toeplitz operators on these spaces.

Large-scale conversational AI systems have become widespread across various sectors. 
One such system, utilized by a research-based company to analyze conversations with customers, has been effectively developed and deployed. 
However, these systems demand substantial data storage space due to their numerous language capabilities, which in turn requires considerable resources to train. 
In order to alleviate these challenges, a cross-lingual model designed for efficient use in a multi-job setup was created. 
This model was trained on a massive dataset consisting of over 1 billion parameters and successfully compressed into a more compact version utilizing efficient training methods. 
Notably, the compressed model maintains its performance levels while also significantly reducing the storage space required for data. 
This innovation has been effectively implemented at Qualtrics, where it has been utilized to power multiple language capabilities.

As data science's prominence grows, access to relevant data has become a major hurdle for researchers and professionals. I'll share my expertise as a data management professional within a research institution, along with personal anecdotes, to help facilitate a deeper understanding of the challenges and perspectives on data access. This chapter aims to offer fresh insights and clarify common issues surrounding controlled, licensed, and open data, along with their respective access mechanisms. By combining fundamental concepts with practical examples, I strive to illuminate the complexities of data access. Ultimately, this piece is intended to serve as a resource guide for research projects facing data access obstacles, as well as a framework for collaboration between data scientists and the global data community.

This research paper investigates the richet isogeny decomposition of the Jacobian varieties associated with certain Riemann surfaces, specifically those of genus three and four, and establishes a link between this decomposition and the generalized Howe curves. We also demonstrate how this leads to new insights into the Galois representation of these Jacobian varieties. Notably, our findings show the Galois group to be an amalgamated free product of cyclic groups, constructed using a specific process involving these curves.

Recent studies suggest that a significant number of hot subdwarf stars exhibit strong magnetic fields. The presence of these magnetic fields in certain hot subdwarfs may be attributed to a merger event involving a white dwarf that underwent magnetic field explosive discharge. A new sample of 12 subdwarf candidates was identified through the analysis of the Gaia DR2 and APOGEE catalogs. The results revealed that three subdwarfs show magnetic field presence while the remaining candidates displayed characteristics of sdB or sdO stars. The magnetic fields of the identified magnetic subdwarfs are discussed, and the discovery of the magnetic subdwarfs in the new sample suggests that magnetic hot subdwarfs are more common than previously thought. The magnetic subdwarfs in the new sample appear to be predominantly metal-deficient, which may be indicative of their origin from galaxy halo populations. The magnetic subdwarfs in the new sample exhibit lower gravity values compared to non-magnetic subdwarfs in the sample, which may be due to the presence of magnetic field-induced magnetic pressure forces. The magnetic subdwarfs in the new sample exhibit lower magnetic field strengths compared to magnetic subdwarfs in previous studies.
