The MFEM library offers a high-order Lagrange interpolation scheme compatible with mixed element discretization. Nonetheless, FELIC's interpolation scheme only supports lower-order discretization. In order to apply Lagrange finite element methods, an interpolation scheme from the higher-order Lagrange basis in MFEM is adapted, and compared to the standard mixed element discretization. The MFEM is then used to solve the Navier-Stokes equations for both mixed and Lagrange schemes, and compared in terms of performance.

We investigate a range of interacting dark energy models, where the interaction rate varies with the evolution of the system. We employ two distinct interaction rate expressions, one proportional to the product of the Hubble rate and dark matter density, and the other proportional to the exponent of the Hubble rate. Our analysis focuses on models where the dark energy equation of state parameter oscillates between -1 and 1, allowing us to identify the nature of these oscillations using the system's Lyapunov exponents. We also use the statefinder diagnostics to differentiate our model from other dark energy models, and numerically calculate the deceleration parameter, equation of state parameter, and interaction rate for each scenario. Our findings indicate that the oscillations in the parameter $w_{\rm DE}$ are of a periodic nature, and the statefinder diagnostics reveal that the system behaves differently at low redshifts in the models based on the Hubble rate expression, but similarly to scalar field models at high redshifts in the models based on the product of the Hubble rate and dark matter density.

Tidal disruption events produce extremely luminous afterglows in the radio spectrum, which initially appeared to contradict expectations. A recent simulation indicates that a shock that forms during the event can be driven by the outflow, producing a powerful cooling effect that accounts for the delayed and prolonged radio emission. A key factor in the shock's effectiveness lies in the orientation of the magnetic field relative to the shock normal, which, when perpendicular, enables efficient particle acceleration into high-energy relativistic electrons emitting synchrotron radiation. A model incorporating the shock's complex geometry and the interstellar medium's density has been developed to fit observed radio light curves of the event ASASSN-15ohl (ASASSN-15ohl).

This research examines the movement of 1-$\mu\rm m$ diameter polystyrene micro-spheres suspended in a liquid, subjected to an ultrasonic wave with a 1.5$\rm MHz$ frequency and varying amplitude, applied in both a steady and pulsed manner. We use numerical models that solve the fluid's behavior using the Navier-Stokes equations and the spheres' response through a Hertz spring-damper model. We investigate how the acoustic bubble instability and cavitation phenomena occur and compare our findings to experimental results.

Human stress has significant implications for daily life, particularly in situations where emotional states are crucial. While there are various methods for stress recognition, they often rely on specific scenarios or limited modalities. Our research presents a novel approach to stress identification, utilizing a multi-modal framework that leverages various input sources. Specifically, our model combines audio and electroencephalogram signals to detect stress in drivers, utilizing an additional task to identify emotional states. Notably, our system surpasses single-modal and audio-EEG models with high accuracy, achieving an average f1 score of 0.71 for the test set.

PanGEA, a free, open-source Python toolset, enables researchers to collect
comprehensive semantic data on large indoor and outdoor spaces. It works in
conjunction with RTK-based GPS technology to provide highly accurate location
tracking. Once installed, users simply download the PanGEA Python client and
follow in-depth guidelines to set up the necessary hardware and software
components. Upon activation, the client automatically tracks and maps the
individual's movement, marking the start and end points of collected trajectories
and labeling the paths according to predefined time intervals. Supporting both
Android and iOS devices, PanGEA is also equipped with a user-friendly Android app
and mobile client API, allowing for seamless integration with other apps or
hardware components via Bluetooth. Open-source and freely available, PanGEA
facilitates the creation of large, diverse datasets for machine learning research.

We have re-examined the mass transition process from blue to red galaxies in galaxy clusters using a more accurate model of star formation and explosive events. We incorporated a gravitational wave-driven initial mass function, which adjusts the mass of star clusters and the maximum mass of their central black holes. We also considered the impact of supernova chemical enrichment on the metal content of the intracluster medium. We found that the decrease in the number of blue galaxies is consistent with the predicted effects of varying the initial mass function and supernova explosion rates. We also discovered that the decrease in the number of blue galaxies is more pronounced in smaller galaxy systems. We tested our model against observational data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and found that it accurately predicts the evolution of galaxy populations. We also found that the model's predictions for the number of supernova explosions match the observed number of Type Ia supernovae. We concluded that the initial mass function and supernova explosion rates used in our model are consistent with the observed properties of elliptical galaxies and the cosmic supernova data.

In the realm of image compressive sensing reconstruction, sparse depiction techniques are gaining attention. Unlike traditional natural sparse representations, this approach captures images with a predetermined set of non-zero values, depicting a sparse scene. A previous method utilized a combination of global and local sparse depictions from an image's feature map, but it failed to consider the inherent grouping patterns within features. This led to suboptimal results when dealing with complex textures and noisy inputs. This study proposes a novel approach called Group-based Sparse Depiction, which captures global and local sparse features at a group level, thus mitigating the issues associated with previous methods. It also introduces a non-convex penalty function that effectively incorporates prior knowledge and reduces the difference between depicted and actual images. Experiments demonstrate that this new approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

In the field of dermatology, accurately detecting skin lesions is a critical challenge. Our research focuses on developing an image-to-text system that can translate natural language descriptions into a detailed list of skin problems. To address this issue, we introduce a multi-task learning approach that incorporates an attention-based model and a loss function to improve the recognition of subtle skin lesions. We also propose an object-by-object learning method that enables the model to learn from individual skin lesions, resulting in superior performance compared to state-of-the-art models. The evaluation results reveal that our model, RethNet, achieves significant advancements in detecting skin lesions, particularly a 9.1% improvement in mean average precision. The model's code will be shared for open research purposes.

Research has shown that low-weight, consecutive degree codes are effective in transmission and processing tasks. This study investigates the performance of consecutive degree codes when used in conjunction with two different decoding methods, say the primary and secondary decoder, where the primary decoder attempts maximum likelihood decoding and the secondary decoder performs list decoding in case of errors. We establish that for a given maximum likelihood error probability, list decoding is successful if this probability, squared, times the number of decoder candidates does not exceed 1. We also determine the code parameters for specific channel conditions and evaluate the computational complexity of consecutive degree codes, observing that their computational requirements can be substantial for certain degree sequences.

Online recommendation systems can expose users to new content and enhance their overall experience. A key feature of these systems is the suggestion list displayed on the dashboard, allowing users to sample and discover items before making explicit ratings. However, users with no existing ratings are considered "cold-start" users, whose preferences are difficult to predict. A common approach is to create a recommendation list based on the transition probabilities from previously rated items to newly rated items. A proposed method called MetaTL uses a two-step learning process to estimate these transition probabilities, resulting in significant improvements over traditional methods that rely on a fixed time horizon.

UHGs, or galaxies with extremely high cosmic ray energies, hold a key place in understanding how galaxies generate and accelerate cosmic rays. A comprehensive analysis of UHGs is provided, focusing on their place within galaxy classification systems, theoretical explanations for their exceptional cosmic ray production, and the potential for future research in this area. UHGs are particularly significant in astrophysical research as they enable scientists to study cosmic ray acceleration in environments similar to those of powerful sources (such as supernova remnants and galaxy clusters) but with much higher productivity. A review of existing theories and observations is conducted, which includes the use of UHGs as a tool to understand cosmic ray properties. A discussion of future research opportunities is also presented, particularly regarding the feasibility of using UHGs to study particle physics.

Understanding momentum transfer during high-speed impacts is crucial for developing a collision theory that can be applied in real-life scenarios, such as deflecting an asteroid. Theoretical collision models have often made the simplifying assumption that the impactor and target are spherical objects. This study examines how the assumed shape of the impactor influences computational predictions of momentum transfer in a molecular dynamics simulation. The results indicate that using different shapes can lead to 20-30% discrepancies in momentum transfer estimates. The findings suggest that using a spherical impactor can underestimate momentum transfer compared to using a more accurate polyhedral shape. This study's results have implications for the Double Asteroid Redirect Vehicle (DART) mission, which relies on a high-speed impact to waterize the asteroid Dimorphos.

This study introduces the Mertens Unfolded Network (MU-Net), a cutting-edge computer vision system for identifying drivers through car windshields. Building on the latest advancements in neural networks and high dynamic range image processing, our proposed MU-Net outperforms existing state-of-the-art image processing techniques and recognition models. A comprehensive evaluation was conducted using three established real-world datasets, resulting in highly accurate high dynamic range image combinations and exceptional driver recognition capabilities.

This study presents an extensive collection of 413 programming language repositories from the Open Source GitHub network, which were analyzed to uncover the underlying design patterns of open source software repositories, particularly in the context of those for programming languages. Our analysis reveals a unique set of community-driven design patterns that set apart language repositories from other types of open source repositories. Our findings suggest that these design patterns differ significantly from those of open source software repositories, highlighting the need for establishing a distinct set of guidelines for designing programming language repositories.

This study introduces a novel class of multistage estimation techniques for
models dealing with both unobserved variables and incomplete response data. 
We establish the existence of these estimators and provide a method for
calculating expectations in the defined model. Furthermore, we propose a
two-stage least squares estimator in the presence of missing outcomes and
incomplete observations on covariates. We assess the performance of this
estimator under various scenarios and compare it with competing methods. Additionally,
we create a simulation study to evaluate the efficiency of our approach.

The complete elliptic integral of the first kind, denoted as $K(m)$ with the parameter $0 < m < 1$, has numerous approximations expressed in terms of inverse hyperbolic tangent. This note focuses on the most recent and efficient approximation discovered by the author, which was presented in a paper published in the Journal of Applied Mathematics and Computing in 2016. We demonstrate that this new approximation is indeed the optimal one for the given parameter range when the value of $m$ is within the specified range, particularly close to 1. This approximation has significant implications for the field of computational physics and can be accessed through a publicly available Wolfram Mathematica package.

This research introduces a novel learning approach for developing control policies solely based on observing process dynamics, without the need for reward functions or direct supervision. A theoretical framework is developed to identify the space of policies derived from decomposing the process into basic actions, as well as the corresponding reward functions necessary to achieve optimal performance. The approach is then adapted for use in reinforcement learning environments with sparse or absent reward feedback using a decomposition-based method. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through its application in various real-world scenarios, including robotic arm control, billiards gameplay, and financial market trading.

The widespread distribution of false information on social media and news platforms has given rise to an urgent need for tools capable of detecting manipulated propaganda and misinformation. This study focuses on the impact of language complexities on the machine's ability to identify manipulated online content. Specifically, we investigate the detection of manipulated news in Arabic using an extensive dataset of 102,548 tweets. Our contributions include the design of two Arabic datasets, MANSYM and MANENG, featuring machine-generated symmetrical and engagement-based variations of manipulated texts, as well as machine learning models that outperform existing benchmarks in detection and generation. Furthermore, we analyze the influence of language difficulties on detection and identify machine translation's role in generating or spreading manipulated content.

A recent publication, "Torsion subgroups of rational elliptic curves over the combination of all $D_4$ extensions of the rational numbers," contained an unintentional error which we aim to correct. In the initial paper, specific instances of $D_4$-extensions were misclassified, thereby contributing to a calculation error in the total number of rational elliptic curves possessing a torsion subgroup of order 32. Notably, this error resulted in an overcount of 12 particular curves, each of which is associated with a 2-parameter elliptic curve. This correction will also involve the explicit identification of these curves, along with a method for determining whether their associated torsion subgroup has a 16-rank greater than or equal to 1 or exactly 1.

In complex quantum systems, nonlocal correlations are crucial for specific tasks, such as verifying proper quantum state preparation and determining the boundaries between quantum and classical realms. We developed a method using matrix product operators to analyze and simulate multiqubit correlations in noisy systems containing up to 60 qubits. Utilizing this approach, we investigated numerous types of decoherence, including the role of nonlocality in preserving entanglement, the impact on Bell inequalities, and the phenomenon of sudden intraqubit dynamics.

In various web domains, such as static web sites and interactive web applications, a single entry point like a home page often contains links leading to content that can't be crawled effectively by traditional methods due to their state-dependent nature. To address this limitation, a novel targeted crawling approach is proposed that uses a policy tree to balance the state-dependent links into manageable sections at different depths. This approach is then applied to target specific web application user interfaces, and a reinforcement learning method is used to optimize the policy tree structure. Experimental results show that the approach effectively addresses the state-dependent link problem and the learned policy tree enhances crawling efficiency and completes the task more effectively compared to conventional crawling methods.

The adoption of object-centric event current (OCEAN) systems has accelerated due to the escalating need to monitor and analyze interconnected systems in real-time, which are increasingly omnipresent. OCEAN systems gather and disseminate real-time information regarding multiple entities and their interactions within a network. In our research, we introduce a computational framework that formalizes the concept of OCEAN systems. This framework provides a methodical approach for defining the inherent characteristics of OCEAN system entities, their interactions, and associated data. Furthermore, we propose a formalized theory of type systems for OCEANTypes, which enables users to specify OCEAN system data in an explicit and structured manner. By leveraging this theory, users can automate the identification of data inconsistencies within OCEAN systems and seamlessly map OCEAN data into relational models.

A novel method for reducing the computational cost of wavefield restoration is introduced, combining the benefits of compactness in the Fourier domain and high-accuracy in the time domain. This approach, based on truncated matrix factorizations, utilizes a limited number of orthonormal factors to approximate an invertible, compact matrix - typically the Fourier transform - in the problem's core. By doing so, the method achieves a significant reduction in the number of rows and columns in the associated weighted Fourier-domain least-squares matrix, from N to N squared times the number of orthonormal factors. Furthermore, the linear system can be solved in the Fourier domain, and the resulting data can be efficiently transformed into the time domain for further processing. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on synthetic data generated from real seismic sources, achieving substantial acceleration while preserving high-quality images.

Metalenses have garnered significant attention for their ability to manipulate light with compact, planar devices that integrate beam shaping, sensing, and imaging functionalities into traditional optical systems. Howeverzeit Nevertheless, their widespread adoption is hindered by limitations such as narrow bandwidth, limited deflection angles, and narrow fields of view. In this research, we demonstrate that metalenses featuring quadratic phase profiles can achieve wide deflection angles and large fields of view while maintaining high field transmission levels across a broad spectrum. Furthermore, we experimentally demonstrate that these metalenses can produce images with high resolution and depth information across a wide spectrum spanning from visible light to the near infrared, thereby opening new avenues for applications such as three-dimensional imaging, microscopy, and optical communication.

Our research examines the behavior of a complex, non-neutral atmospheric pressure plasma jet system, comprising a plasma source, gas, and tubular confinement. We analyze the interaction of electrons, ions, and neutrals within its components, using numerical simulations to replicate its operation. These simulations reveal that the plasma source behaves similarly to a vacuum when not energized, but exhibits unique behavior when energized. We develop a simplified model to explain this difference, focusing on the plasma source's interaction with background gas on the tube's axis. By accounting for the plasma source's influence, we can account for the observed behavior.

This study investigates the impact of string corrections on black holes in d-dimensional space, focusing specifically on quasi-normal modes within the framework of geodesic perturbation theory and the eikonal approximation. The analysis reveals that string corrections decrease the frequency of perturbation oscillations, while also increasing their damping rate. The outcome is more pronounced in higher dimensional space, which makes it more resilient to various modifications of black holes. The influence of string corrections on the shadow of black holes is demonstrated through null geodesics, while numerical calculations provide further insights into the astrophysical implications of string corrections on black hole quasi-normal modes.

A time delay caused by differences in light travel times along the two paths of a gravitational wave is expected to result in a loss of signal in pulsar timing array searches. Two methods used to mitigate this effect, the common-spectrum and cross-correlation methods, differ in their approach: the common-spectrum method applies a filter to account for the expected time delay, while the cross-correlation method discards data based on differences in travel time. To determine which method is more effective, we simulated the signal from a gravitational wave and compared the efficiency of each method. The results show that the cross-correlation method performs better and depends less on the timing accuracy of the pulsars on average. However, both methods suffer from a significant loss of signal due to differences in travel time, indicating that future searches with improved signal processing and high-precision pulsar timing, may benefit from alternative methods such as frequency-averaging.

The necessity of finding suitable generator polynomials for error-correcting codes is well-established in theory and practice. In this study, we propose a new approach to determine a necessary and sufficient condition for a polynomial to act as a generator matrix in a support-constrained code. By leveraging properties of the univariate nodal domain polynomials derived from a graph called the Gilbert-Hammersley-Welch graph, we provide a more efficient method for generator matrix search. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the resulting support-constrained codes maintain several beneficial properties, including self-dual codes and skew-symmetric weight distributions.

This paper examines truncated Toeplitz operators based on symbols with a specific form, where the symbols are a sum of two parts: a bounded function and a bounded operator, and the operator component contains a cut-off region that does not extend beyond $|z| < R$, where $R$ is a positive real number. The study reveals that, under certain conditions, the symbols can be extended to form equivalent operators within a specific set of symbols, even when the operator component does not adhere to a specific property called contractive. The research further shows that, in the context of certain spaces, the extended operators exhibit contractive behavior. The study also demonstrates the feasibility of approximating these extended operators using a sequence of equivalent operators, where the approximating operators have symbols that form a specific sequence.

In high-stakes therapeutic fields, where treatments can have severe consequences, as in cancer therapy, or delicate effects, where small changes matter, as in materials science, precision is often crucial.  Sequential trials designed to evaluate multiple treatments at once can be particularly valuable in these contexts, as they allow researchers to adjust their approach mid-process, using only the available data to guide them. One key advantage of these trials is the ability to adjust the test results, taking into account uncertainty, as a Bayesian filter would. Although Bayesian methods have gained acceptance in therapeutic contexts, where the goal is to evaluate the treatments themselves, they have yet to gain traction in high-impact fields, where the focus is often on detecting a difference in treatment impact. This paper aims to highlight the benefits of Bayesian methods in both therapeutic and high-impact contexts, exploring how they can be adapted and improved.

The primary objective of anomaly detection is to identify anomalies from normal instances, and research indicates that unsupervised machine learning is particularly effective at achieving this goal. Nevertheless, there is a significant challenge associated with anomaly detection, and that is the issue of domain shift, which can be attributed to variations in data collection patterns or changes in underlying distributions over time. In our study, we investigate the potential of Uplift Mapping Analysis (UMAP) as a visualisation tool to facilitate the analysis of data evolution and detect anomalies under domain-shift conditions. By utilizing the NUSTAR challenge dataset, we simulate a real-world scenario where instances are collected at different times and locations, and evaluate the effectiveness of UMAP in capturing patterns of data evolution. Our findings demonstrate that UMAP-generated embeddings can be used to accurately detect anomalies and provide insights into the underlying data distributions.

Theoretically, a three-dimensional dilute gas of $SU(N)$ fermions is investigated when interactions are either below or at the point of the Mott transition. Unlike $SU(N=2)$, where magnetic order forms in the ground state due to the presence of a ferromagnetic channel, this study reveals that magnetic properties in the ground state are governed by the presence of various spin channels. At low temperatures, when interactions are stronger than the critical value, they become relevant and induce a spontaneous breaking of U(1) symmetry, while at the transition point, they become relevant at the same rate as the U(1) mode. This theoretical framework is used to analyze the behavior of these systems near the transition point and to calculate the specific heat due to the breaking of U(1) symmetry at finite temperatures.

The primary goal of our study is to utilize machine learning to categorize known gamma-ray pulsars into their respective classes based on their characteristics. To accomplish this, we used the COSMIC pipeline to compile a dataset consisting of 14 features from 433 gamma-ray pulsars. Utilizing the PyStack package, we employed a variety of machine learning algorithms to identify the most effective ones. Following a rigorous evaluation, we discovered that gradient boosting, a subset of machine learning, yielded the most accurate classification results, specifically 92% in our best-case scenario. In addition, we expanded our dataset by incorporating 67 previously classified gamma-ray middle-aged pulsars and successfully categorized 63 of them, while identifying 9 as unknown. To further validate our approach, we used machine learning to predict the $P/\dot{P}$ plane and successfully identified known millisecond pulsars, specifically those with values in the range of 0.1 to 10 years. Our study has significant implications for understanding the data distribution in the $P/\dot{P}$ plane and the distribution of pulsars in the plane.

The predicted existence of fractional quantum Hall states at multiple filling thresholds is a common phenomenon in experiments. However, the underlying theory fails to account for distinct magnetoroton branches, causing total rules to be insufficient in explaining system behavior. The presence of magnetorotons and total state rules are crucial for describing experimental results, and our research provides a theoretical framework to calculate these branches. The associated energy gaps are found to be highly dependent on system size and particle density. Furthermore, the study reveals that magnetorotons can lead to either particle or hole rich states, and in experiments, the dominant state type influences system behavior. The total state rule, incorporating magnetorotons, is established to provide a more comprehensive understanding of integer quantum Hall plateaus.

The network of multipurpose Telescopes for UV, Visible and UV-X-ray photodetectors (TUVVUs) in Russia, India, Bulgaria, and Mexico, known as Extreme Energy Events (E3), has been operational since 2015 within the EAS-TOP/HD-MTA/IN2P3/ICNPI/ICR research project. Comprising over 100 telescopes with various formats, sizes, and sensitivity levels, the E3 network spans more than 4,000 meters and covers nine longitudes. This article provides an in-depth examination of the telescopes' key features, focusing on their basic components, data acquisition systems, and performance characteristics.

The Cauchy problem for the truncated Boltzmann equation is studied with a focus on its applicability to gas mixtures where collisions involve multiple molecules. To address this, a systematic method is developed to validate the equation's uniqueness and stability, assuming data meet certain smallness criteria and are related to a singular initial configuration. The method applies universally, not just for mixtures but any general collision processes, and can be extended to study non-linear integro-differential equations.

The prevalence of classifiers has led to widespread adoption across many significant tasks like self-driving cars and image recognition. Although common in many applications, the data used to train these classifiers may contain inaccurately labeled information. In situations where data is annotated by humans, the assessment of the training set quality is typically based on the assumption that the label set is error-free. However, the risk of noisy data is particularly pronounced in learning from crowdsourced information. In this study, we evaluate the effectiveness of classifiers developed from noisy data by employing a triple approach: (1) examining the influence of label corruption on the performance of standard classifiers, (2) assessing the efficacy of existing noise detection and correction methods that are often used in conjunction with classifiers, and (3) investigating a new technique for learning robust classifiers that can perform well even with label noise, noise detection, and correction. Our experiments demonstrate that these new classifiers can deliver superior results and are more resilient to noisy data than standard classifiers.

This research focuses on automorphism groups of one code that are embedded in the group of automorphisms of another, larger code. Specifically, we analyze how the automorphism group of a orbit code is a subgroup of the automorphism group of its defining code. Additionally, we investigate the symmetries inherent in key scheduling schemes that create orbit codes, with a view of enhancing security by identifying and excluding automorphism groups that could be used to derive structural information about the code from its corresponding key.

A precise mass measurement for a star at the cluster turnoff in M67 has been achieved through a combination of spectroscopic and photometric data, leading to the identification of its location in the H-R diagram. The star's position on the cluster sequence in the H-R diagram confirms it is a member of M67. The analysis yielded a fundamental mass for the star of $1.236 \pm 0.043 M_{\odot}$ based on the parallax from Gaia EDR3 and the mean radial velocity of the cluster. The derived mass is in agreement with the expected mass from the location of the star on the H-R diagram and the age of the cluster as determined from the parallax. The derived mass is also in agreement with the expected mass based on the expected mass-radius relation for the star's effective temperature. The analysis also yielded precise values for the bolometric magnitude and luminosity of the star, which are consistent with the expected values based on the effective temperature.

The collection of all eigenfunctions can be formed for the complex Schrödinger equation, $\mathscr{L}_c(x) = -\partial^2\!/\!\partial x^2 + cx^\alpha$, where $c$ is real, and $\alpha$ is a non-negative, odd number. For values of $\alpha$ greater than or equal to 3, eigenfunctions become bounded as $x$ approaches infinity, and for $\alpha$ equal to 1 or 2, eigenfunctions form a closed, complex vector space over the real or complex number system.

SPH is a mesh-free Lagrangian method that's particularly useful for modeling fluid dynamics. It's known for its ease of use, as it resolves the nodes' positions directly without needing to reconfigure a mesh. With SPH, the volume of control volumes is calculated by integrating the density with specific weights, as opposed to calculating the area of boundaries using integrals of velocities or gradients. This approach breaks down into two main issues: accurately determining the boundaries of the spheres and calculating the gradients of the velocities. This research presents a new method for defining sphere boundaries that's based on particles' densities, as opposed to using the condition of equal density. It also introduces a new estimate for the gradient of the velocities, which is based on density and has a proven consistency and convergence theory. This approach has been tested in various scenarios, including the movement of a sphere through a stationary fluid, the Oran's disk impact test, and the simulation of a 2D dam break. The results show that the new method for calculating the boundaries is consistent and that the new gradient estimator is accurate and efficient.

Recent advancements in deep learning-based spectral imaging technologies have been significant, enabling high-resolution spectral data acquisition. Nevertheless, the high cost of spectral sensors remains a major obstacle to their widespread adoption. To mitigate this challenge, the proposed research focuses on developing an efficient algorithm for spectral super-resolution, utilizing data from low-resolution spectral sensors and a color camera. The proposed algorithm, a Pixel-Aware Deep Function-blend Network (PADFNet), addresses the inherent differences between spectral and color image characteristics, incorporating a pixel-aware attention module to capture spatial variations in these images. The network's hierarchical structure allows for end-to-end learning of high-resolution spectral images and the prediction of pixel-level spectral energies. The PADFNet model is trained on extensive datasets and demonstrated to outperform competing deep learning methods through extensive experiments.

Item geotagging is the process of assigning a location to an object or point of interest based on available data. This study examines a novel method for identifying and linking the locations of points of interest, such as shops, to specific objects within images captured by Street View cameras. The approach relies on a model that integrates camera position data with image metadata, allowing for the association of points of interest with relevant street-level imagery. The proposed framework demonstrates substantial potential for geotagging existing points of interest, assuming relevant image coverage, and has the potential to significantly enhance geotagging accuracy by learning from existing points of interest, resulting in improved accuracy.

The scale and complexity of water storage in reservoirs, particularly in large systems, underscores their significance in the water cycle. Smaller dams in Africa often play a vital role in local economies by providing water for drinking, energy, agriculture, industry, and urban areas. These dams are crucial infrastructure that require effective management to mitigate risks associated with flooding, pollution, and safety. To this end, accurately mapping and identifying small dams in Africa is a pressing need. To this end, a novel approach using metric learning techniques is proposed to locate small dams in Africa using satellite imagery. Specifically, a self-supervised method is employed that does not require prior knowledge of dam locations. These techniques have been applied to identify dams in Africa with an area of at least 0.05 ha across multiple satellite images from 1995, 2000, 2015, 2020, and 2021. The results show that the proposed method is effective in localizing small dams in remote areas.
This paper establishes the concept of a QFS-region and examines its characteristics.

The 'point-of-attraction' refers to the location where an individual feels most drawn, often influenced by both textual and visual cues in social media content. Determining POI types, such as 'beach', 'city', or'mountain', can help us better understand user preferences and attractiveness ratings for any given location. This study introduces a POI type classification system that combines text and image analysis to better grasp the attract points of various locations. This system will be instrumental in enhancing recommendations tailored to individual user preferences and can also contribute valuable insights for theoretical and practical applications.

Investors rely on public disclosures, including financial reports and company announcements, as key sources of information for making investment decisions. However, company leaders also play a significant role in shaping market perceptions through their participation in conference calls following quarterly earnings releases. In this research, we delve into the relationship between conference call transcripts and market-driven stock price movements. By utilizing market reactions to specific phrases or topics discussed during these calls, we found that certain words and themes can effectively predict subsequent stock price fluctuations, highlighting the substantial impact of corporate communication on market sentiment.

The issue of limited battery power in sensor networks has led to the emergence of the minimum energy per node problem, where the goal is to minimize the total energy usage under a limited total power constraint. This problem is computationally intractable, but a feasible solution can be obtained through the analysis of the coverage area of the sensors and by determining the optimal number of active sensors. This paper presents a novel approach to minimize energy usage in sensor networks with varying node capabilities, and through the use of the SIC and LIC models, it is able to obtain precise solutions to the problem. These models allow the optimization of the network's performance, yielding near-optimal results that approach the optimal solution as the number of active sensors approaches infinity.

We have developed a quantum-inspired filtering technique to accurately estimate a quantum state from a linear combination of known states and an unknown coefficient. Our method relies on a variational quantum algorithm combined with a classical optimization process and a quadratic programming library. This approach not only achieves optimal performance through convex optimization but also demonstrates superior results compared to existing quantum annealing based methods in solving large-scale linear systems.

Infant skyrmions, initially introduced as topological defects in thin layers, 
exhibit unique properties and can be identified by distinct textures and energy 
density patterns. In our study, we explore the formation of compact self-dual 
gauged infant skyrmions in nonlinear media by applying the Skyrme model with a 
gauged term, and we analyze their behavior in two-dimensional and three-dimensional 
settings. By examining the energy distribution, we observe that the compact infant 
skyrmion's energy is confined within a spherical boundary, mirroring the Skyrme-Faddeev 
soliton in its two-dimensional form and a sphere within a three-dimensional sphere, 
in a three-dimensional setting.

This report summarizes our research efforts, which involve conducting comprehensive studies on four-fermion final states in the SMEFT framework at the LHC, along with exploring novel electron-photon interactions at J-Park and CLFAS accelerators.

We have created an underwater nuclear magnetic compass that relies on nitrogen-14 atomic spins in a diamond environment, utilizing spin-rotation-resonance techniques to control and read the spins of the diamond. A single nitrogen-14 atomic spin's state can be detected with near-perfect accuracy using room temperature measurements. Our device allows for precise measurements of electron and nuclear spin interactions within diamond, as well as the effects of external magnetic fields on the nitrogen-14 atomic spins. In an isotopic-enriched diamond with more stable atomic spins, we demonstrate a diamond nuclear magnetic compass with improved sensitivity, surpassing existing rubidium atomic compasses by about two orders of magnitude in magnetic field resolution when operated at room temperature.

Cellular behavior is shaped by the dynamic interactions between the various components it's made of, and accurately simulating these processes is essential for understanding how cells function and responding to experimental data. Although progress has been slow in developing a unifying framework for in silico cell modeling, significant advancements have been made in recent years that bring us closer to this goal. In this review, we explore the challenges involved in creating a comprehensive in silico cell model and provide an overview of the emerging methods and principles that will help overcome these obstacles.

Picture search, a crucial component in e-commerce, enables customers to quickly locate products. Current picture search methods are designed for stationary queries, yet they are ineffective for scenarios where the image of the target object is captured using a mobile device. The challenge lies in that a single image cannot capture the complete object, resulting in poor search results when a single snapshot is used as the query. To address this issue, we propose a multi-view picture search system that allows users to capture and combine multiple views of the object into a single query, thereby significantly improving search results. To facilitate this process, we developed a scalable multi-view search engine that integrates multi-view queries and provides accurate results. The system consists of three key components: a multi-view search engine, a multi-view prediction module, and a mobile multi-view client. The multi-view search engine utilizes a novel index to efficiently process multi-view queries, while the mobile multi-view client utilizes a software agent to capture and combine views. Experimental results indicate that the proposed system can significantly reduce the search time by 10 times and result in a 5-10 fold decrease in the number of relevant items returned.

Epilepsy impacts one in 26 of the global population, with seizures causing sudden muscle spasms due to abnormal brain activity levels that can evolve over time. Timely detection of seizures can alleviate their physical consequences and enhance the patient's overall well-being. However, detecting seizures can be challenging due to variations in the individual's medical and personal environment. A promising approach is the use of Hyperdimensional Computing, a novel computing framework that can learn complex patterns efficiently and adapt to changing data distributions. Our research investigates the effectiveness of HD computing in improving seizure detection rates, particularly in novel patients, through various strategies such as combining multiple seizure feature sets and using novel patients as training data for individual patients, as well as incorporating environmental factors. Our findings show that these strategies can lead to a significant improvement in detection accuracy, with a maximum gain of 9.9% in detection rates compared to traditional methods, especially in novel patients, without requiring additional training or sample time.

The detection of binary black holes by the Deci-hertz observatory will provide the first gravitational wave standard sirens with specific astrophysical locations. This will enable the estimation of the Hubble constant with minimal uncertainty and will be influenced by the uncertainty in the Hubble constant itself. A study has been conducted on how the uncertainty in the Hubble constant affects the location of binary black holes in this context. This has also led to the development of a method to correct for this uncertainty using the Hubble constant's measured value. This correction method has been tested and has shown that it can improve the precision of the Hubble constant's inference by a factor of 2.5, assuming that the Hubble constant's true value is 67.32 Gbps/kilometer, and the detection rate of 1000 standard sirens from binary black holes. This has also shown that the detection rate of 1000 standard sirens can be increased by 0.1% for every 0.1% uncertainty in the Hubble constant. This has also led to the development of a method to correct for the uncertainty in the Hubble constant's measurement using the gravitational wave standard sirens. This method has been tested and has shown that it can improve the precision of the Hubble constant's inference by a factor of 1.3.

We have established a multilingual dataset known as QALD-9-plus that incorporates English queries along with 18 non-English queries translated by native speakers, utilizing diverse texts. Unlike the original QALD-9 dataset which drew queries from the DBpedia SPARQL example query set, we selected queries from the DBpedia resource and linked sources, particularly focusing on diverse types of questions. The test queries in all languages are evaluated against both DBpedia and Wikidata resources, providing valuable insights into the performance of both systems and specific challenges in handling the DBpedia resource. The QALD-9-plus dataset is particularly significant for the evaluation of English, giving researchers a chance to compare their results against both a state-of-the-art benchmark and a language-specific high-performing system. We also provide results from the participants of the 2016 QALC shared task and their respective baselines, indicating the effectiveness of multilingual approaches in handling the DBpedia resource.

We introduce a new framework, Executive Function, that tackles the problem of sampling and re-labeling perception data. It views this task as a special state-saving and trajectory-guided reinforcement learning (RL) issue, where the state is a current perception and the goal is to maximize long-term rewards. By incorporating a memory that stores the experiences and a unique RL agent, Executive Function addresses this problem. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through significant improvements in learning a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) on the Street View Sequence (SVS) dataset, outperforming traditional re-labeling methods. Furthermore, our approach is compatible with various RL algorithms and can be applied to other state-saving and trajectory-guided RL problems.

Artificial intelligence has significant potential to revolutionize healthcare through medical image analysis, but its effectiveness depends on the reliability of the data used to train models.  We must ensure that the data used to train AI systems does not contain inherent biases that compromise the accuracy and fairness of the resulting models.  In an effort to address this issue, we have developed an innovative framework that detects and assesses biases present in medical image datasets.  We apply this framework to two well-established eye disease datasets, discovering that they contain inherent biases that could negatively impact the performance of AI models trained on this data.  Our findings highlight the need for increased scrutiny of the data used to train models in this field and provide a foundation for developing more equitable AI solutions in healthcare.

Many real-world scenarios require the implementation of accurate metric learning techniques, but noisy training data can significantly hinder their performance. A common approach to addressing this challenge involves incorporating a robust and resilient method that effectively eliminates unreliable samples. This paper introduces the Smooth Proxy-Anchors with Cost filters (SPAC) technique, which combines a novel cost filter with proxy anchors to assess the reliability of training samples. The proposed SPAC model is characterized by three key components: the estimation of proxy anchor centers using clean data, the generation of proxy anchors, and the construction of cost functions that measure the distance between query and prototype vectors. The SPAC model employs a smooth proxy-anchoring strategy, which assigns a higher cost to query vectors farther from their corresponding prototypes. Additionally, the integration of a robustness constraint in the loss function ensures that the SPAC model is more resilient to noisy data. The proposed SPAC model is demonstrated to outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in noisy data scenarios, both in both clean and noisy datasets.

The clustering properties of dark matter halos are commonly analyzed using the average separation between halo pairs, typically weighted by their mass ratio. We propose an alternative weighting approach that gives greater emphasis to high-mass pairs, thus focusing on the more massive halo within each pair. We find that this weighted measure, known as the density gradient weighted association function, is a more sensitive probe of cosmological parameters, particularly when analyzing galaxy surveys like the SDSS. By utilizing a mock galaxy catalog, we examine the effect of different volume limits and find that the weighted association function can distinguish between two cosmological models with similar maximum halo masses, such as the Planck XIII and WMAP-9 models.

A theoretical framework of topological superfluidity is developed, where the underlying structure of the associated phase is analyzed. This framework posits that the superfluidity arises from a constrained system consisting of bosons in a two-dimensional space with SU(5) symmetry, which breaks down down to U(1)×U(1), enabling a detailed analysis of the superfluid's phase. The theory is refined by incorporating a specific constraint, which leads to the emergence of a U(1) symmetry and allows for the derivation of topological orders. The theory is then adapted to a model of superfluidity with a single constraint, resulting in the derivation of topological orders consistent with the known properties of the topological insulator in (2+1) dimensions. The study concludes by suggesting that this model could serve as a basis for understanding the SO(5) superfluidity in the 1D system of CePy.

Micro-Phosphor Array Detectors, also known as MAPD, are a type of photodetector that features a surface with a uniform, low surface area coverage of phosphor particles, typically measuring under 1 micrometer in diameter, resulting in fast signal processing and high precision time resolution, making them suitable for the detection of low-intensity signals, such as those in single-photon applications. However, the efficiency of MAPD decreases when detecting high-energy photons, resulting in a reduced signal. To address this limitation, researchers have proposed an alternative concept, SnowStorm, which involves applying a thin, uniform coating of phosphors to a photodetector surface, expanding MAPD's range to include detection of high-energy photons, while retaining the performance advantages of MAPD.

Let $R$ be an admissible ring. This study focuses on the curved genus, $\gen R(\mathbb{D}_1,\ldots,\mathbb{D}_n)$, which represents the dimension of the $i$th Kurke's curve ring. We establish the Gorenstein rings conditions under which $\gen R(\mathbb{D}_1,\ldots,\mathbb{D}_i)$ equals one for a specific index $i$. Furthermore, this work investigates the properties of the $\mathcal{L}_n(R)$ family, specifically proving that for a Cohen-Macaulay ring, the inverse limit of $\mathcal{L}_n(R)$ equals the local ring of $R$ and also the projective dimension of $R$ equals one for all prime ideals when each $\mathcal{L}_n(R)$ is Cohen-Macaulay.

A comprehensive investigation into the temperature-dependent magnetic phase transitions of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ at varying pressures was conducted using nuclear forward scattering (NFS). At zero pressure, the material follows a specific thermal ordering, characterized by an upward shift in transition temperature with slight temperature variations. Pressure applications lead to distinct changes in the material's thermal ordering pattern, as observed in experiments up to 6.2 GPa and theoretical calculations. Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ exhibits a complex first-order magnetic phase transition at ambient pressure, but shows a second-order transition under elevated pressure. Notably, the transition temperature increases with pressure, and the material's magnetic phase shifts from a first-order to a second-order transition as pressure is applied. These findings have implications for the material's potential use in magnetic devices that operate at elevated pressures.

A new, data-driven trading approach, called TrExpanse, has been developed to evaluate the costs of brokerage services. This approach considers both the trading algorithm's performance and the costs incurred due to fees, slippage, and trading session disruptions. Utilizing a Bayesian framework, the method estimates the unknown parameters of the cost components based on the observed equity curves of the trading strategies. A statistical analysis is then conducted to compare the trading performance and costs associated with multiple brokerages, as well as different trading sessions. TrExpanse has been successfully tested using a dataset comprising a diversified set of quantitative trading strategies that interact with the Xing Position, a large brokerage platform. The findings indicate that the trading costs vary significantly across different brokers and trading sessions, and are influenced by factors such as account size, the time of day, and the level of market volatility.

Optomechanical add-drop filters (OM-ADFs) are crucial components in optical communication and network systems. The efficiency of these systems heavily relies on the capabilities of the optical connections linking the ADFs together. The efficiency of optical connections can be significantly enhanced with fully adjustable optomechanical add-drop filters, which allow for precise wavelength control. In this research, we present a design for an OM-ADF that utilizes a specific type of optical cavity called a hybrid optical cavity or a optomechanical Michelson interferometer. The proposed design features two optical cavities, each with a high reflectivity mirror and a variable reflectivity mirror, which enables accurate wavelength control. The effectiveness of this design was demonstrated through simulations.

Public health interventions are being implemented in response to pandemics, however the impact on general public behavior is being monitored using various health and disease indicators. Social distancing measures have been shown to reduce the spread of highly contagious diseases such as COVID-19, but assessing their effectiveness can be a challenging task. To evaluate the effect of an intervention on disease transmission, an alternative method must be used to compare disease prevalence before and after the intervention is put into effect. Public health records, including information on hospital visits, X-rays, and death certificates, can provide valuable data on disease trends. To determine the effectiveness of an intervention, a comparison of disease incidence and mortality rates before and after it was put into effect is necessary. To achieve this, researchers can utilize data from publicly available sources, including Web content, to compare disease patterns and assess the effectiveness of an intervention. To illustrate this process, a case study on the COVID-19 pandemic is presented, in which disease incidence and mortality rates were extracted from online sources, including news articles and government reports. To compare disease patterns before and after the intervention was put into effect, a case study of New York State, California, and Colorado was conducted. To assess the effectiveness of an intervention, a case study on the COVID-19 pandemic in New York State, California, and Colorado is being conducted.

A novel image compression framework, PILC, is presented which leverages end-to-end learning capabilities on a GPU. By utilizing a non-learnable, conventional bitstream structure in combination with an unadultered learnable significance encoding process, high compression ratios are achieved while guaranteeing lossless quality. This framework is substantiated by a substantial 100K-image dataset, comprising the entirety of the Wikimedia Commons public domain image collection. PILC's effectiveness is showcased through comparative evaluations with established image compressors, notably with regard to inherent characteristics such as speed, efficiency in low-bandwidth scenarios, and resilience to errors during transmission.

The first measurement of branching ratios for the decays $B^{+} \to D_s^{+}K^{+}K^{-}$, $B^{0} \to D_s^{0}K^{+}K^{-}$, and $B_s^{0} \to D_s^{0}K^{+}K^{-}$ is presented using $pp$ collision data collected by the LHCb experiment at various energies corresponding to 3.0 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis yields branching fractions of $B^{+} \to D_s^{+}K^{+}K^{-}$ (3.0 %), $B^{0} \to D_s^{0}K^{+}K^{-}$ (0.54 %), and $B_s^{0} \to D_s^{0}K^{+}K^{-}$ (0.47 %) relative to the $B \to D_s^{+}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ decay mode. Furthermore, upper limits are set for the decay $B^{+} \to D_s^{+}\phi$ at the 95% confidence level.

Optimal transport distances are sensitive to even single-point anomalies and often used in distortion measures that prioritize preserving overall structure over details. To address these limitations, we've developed a way to maintain a finite-scale distance that can withstand outliers by incorporating a robust penalty for deviations that exceed a threshold. This results in a robust OT solution that remains efficient despite the presence of anomalies. We demonstrate the practical applications of this robust OT by showing it can be used for two novel tasks: identifying anomalies in datasets and approximating the Wasserstein distance when faced with noisy transport plans.

In this research, we examine the concept of uniquely collaborative (UC) agents who prioritize mutual assistance within teams by supporting other agents when necessary, often resulting in better decision-making. However, the current approach of deriving UC agent policies through minimax optimization leads to agents that are overly passive and rely on human teammates, who are ultimately responsible for effective team outcomes. To address this, we introduce the Human Decision Framework model, which simulates the actions of humans in a team environment, enabling UC agents to develop more collaborative policies through reinforcement learning. Our findings demonstrate that the HD framework model leads to more competitive performance in cooperative 2v2 games and that agents trained on it exhibit more collaborative behavior, including actively contributing to team discussions and forming strategies in conjunction with their human teammates, compared to the conventional minimax-based policy.

We explore the concept of supersymmetry in the context of quantum field theories, specifically focusing on a simplified scenario with a single action of the supersymmetry transformation, denoted as $\q$. This singular action leads to a $9+1$ dimensional spacetime, where time is derived as an invariant measure within a $10$-dimensional spacetime, thereby rendering the action non-supersymmetric in this dimension. We then discuss how to incorporate additional supersymmetry actions, each associated with an independent derivation of the time dimension, resulting in a total of $2^n$ distinct time dimensions in the presence of $n$ such actions. This framework is further illustrated within the context of a simplified $\pho^4$ theory in a $10$-dimensional spacetime with $\pho^2$ potential, where we detail the construction of the corresponding field theory and demonstrate the presence of $n$ supersymmetries for a specific choice of the anticommuting spinor $\q$. We also outline various possible applications of this work, including the extension of this formalism to the Green-Supersymmetry action and its associated implications for the anticommuting spinor $\q$.

This study compares the performance of individuals from diverse professions on a range of tasks through visualizations. We surveyed 101 participants from 18 different professions and had them interpret 12 visualizations while answering questions. Our findings reveal that individuals from various disciplines exhibit similar task performance, contradicting expectations of prior expertise. This discovery aligns with the notion that visualizations effectively convey information to a broad audience. We discovered that 84% of the variance in task performance can be attributed to factors within our study, with demographic characteristics and profession having minimal influence. Furthermore, our study suggests that task instructions play a more significant role in performance than we initially anticipated.

We present a novel proof loop, termed Clause Set Loop, which iteratively refines a set of clauses until it becomes loop-carried in until it reaches a terminating state. This loop can effectively be performed in conjunction with user-provided induction hypotheses, leading us to a method for generating an automated proof procedure that incorporates user-provided induction hypotheses in inductive first-order theorem proving. This proof procedure is demonstrated to be effective through experimental testing.

Graph retrieval is a critical machine learning issue that has garnered significant attention, primarily due to its capacity to tackle complex data challenges such as knowledge graph completion, text graph clustering, and network game modeling, among others. In this paper, we delve into the details of a popular graph retrieval method, examining its corresponding models and their respective strengths and weaknesses. We demonstrate how an existing model can be adapted to resolve a significant drawback and provide a deeper understanding of another model's properties, saving space and enabling more efficient training times.

Deep learning models are often trained using static representations of language, but this approach may limit their ability to capture dynamic patterns in speech. In order to improve the modeling of these complex patterns, researchers have found that training deep learning models on speech data that is deliberately slowed down can improve their ability to capture long-term dependencies in speech. This technique is similar to a technique called "subsampled pretraining" that has been used successfully in language modeling, and it has been shown to improve performance significantly. This work examines the effectiveness of subsampled pretraining and compares it to other techniques that have been used to improve pretraining for speech models. The results show that subsampled pretraining is a highly effective method that significantly outperforms other techniques, and it is particularly effective when applied to slow-moving patterns of speech.

A critical issue in electricity distribution systems is ensuring fair distribution
to consumers, who typically don't have the power to negotiate prices or the amount
of electricity they receive. One approach to achieve fairness is to apply constrained
optimization techniques, which aim to allocate electricity efficiently while meeting
basic power requirements, maxing out capacity, and maintaining fairness across
different consumers. However, a key challenge arises in defining fairness, with
different definitions leading to distinct optimization objectives. Notably, popular
definitions center around minimizing differences among consumers, which can be
complicated by varying consumer needs. To address this, we develop a family of
optimization problems that balance efficiency, fairness, and flexibility, allowing
for multiple interpretations of fairness and accommodating diverse consumer demands.
We provide a general framework for solving these problems using advanced
algorithms, which can be easily adapted to real-world systems. Furthermore, we
show that our proposed framework can be effectively solved using existing
algorithms, which can be efficiently scaled up to handle large, complex systems.
Finally, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the trade-offs between efficiency,
fairness, and flexibility through extensive simulations, which demonstrate the
performance of our proposed framework in real-world scenarios.

The task of coreference resolution focuses on identifying and grouping equivalent entities within a document. We delve into the field of event coreference - a sub-task that involves pinpointing and differentiating events mentioned by various sources. Notably, our focus is on the challenging scenario where the events are referenced by multiple sources, but the text that describes them does not appear identical. To address this challenge in the realm of politics, we have compiled a dataset comprising events discussed by both supportive and opposing news outlets on the same topic. We have developed a neural network-based approach that incorporates both attention-based techniques for text analysis and a BERT model for integrating external knowledge, along with a method for utilizing co-occurrence information among mentioned entities. Through our evaluation, we have found that the proposed approach excels in the realm of event coreference resolution, outperforming current state-of-the-art results by significant margins.

The Complementarity Knapsack Problem, a CNP involving finite and infinite constraints, was initially defined by Koenig et al. to model certain bipartite matching combinatorial optimization problems. This paper focuses on developing sufficient and necessary conditions for determining CNP feasibility using the concept of complementarity polytopes comprised of extreme points initially identified by Kozlov, which were later utilized by Golan and Koenig in their study on complexity, as well as by Golan in her 2021 dissertation.

Given a semiprime ring $\mathscr{S}$ of characteristic not equal to $2$, we define $m, n \in \Bbb{N}_0$ and an integer $r$ with $n \leq r < m$. An $(m, n)$-central element $x$ of the ring is defined as $x^2 = nx^3 - nx^2$. An $(m, n)$-Jordan centralizer is an element $x$ such that the centralizer of $x$ is an $(m, n)$-element. For $r \leq n \leq m$, an $r$-Jordan derivation is an $r$-derivation where $nx^2 = rnx, \forall x \in \mathscr{S}$, and an $r$-Jordan centralizer is an element of this type. An $r$-Jordan derivation is an $(m, n)$-derivation when $r = m$. For $r \geq m$, an $r$-derivation is an $(m, n)$-derivation when $n \leq m$. We will show that all $r$-Jordan derivators and $r$-Jordan centralizers are zero for $r \geq m$, and in the case of a semiprime ring, we will show that all $r$-Jordan derivators and $r$-Jordan central

We validate Weinberg's constraint equations for a massless scalar field's two-parameter interaction, which is derived from the most general Lagrangian, by imposing helicity conservation as a constraint on the scattering matrix in an arbitrary basis. Additionally, the same constraints also give rise to a new set of non-trivial seven-parameter shift- and winding-momentum relations for the most general Lagrangian involving vector, tensor, and spin-3/2 particles.

The transversality of families of nonlinear transformations is examined, and this investigation leads to the identification of specific conditions under which it ensures the existence of a transversal. This existence condition is applicable to a broader range of continuous time systems and serves to extend a known result concerning Favard length for a particular subclass of such systems. The implications of the new existence condition for transversality are then explored in the context of the averaging principle.

We introduce a novel framework that enables training of high-performing controllers using efficient guided policy search methods. This approach integrates a tube model predictive control (TMPC) with a robust dynamic behavior that serves as a reference point for the controller in real-time. The TMPC system, which is only updated at pre-set intervals, acts as a stabilizing guide during online operation. The controller, operating in real-time, strives to emulate the TMPC's dynamic behavior while also learning from it to improve its performance. The framework is particularly advantageous in scenarios where the TMPC is computationally demanding to recalculate at short intervals. The proposed approach is shown to be effective in simulating the dynamics of a quadrotor while minimizing computational costs and outperforming current state-of-the-art methods in a benchmark task.

A theoretical model based on the semi-classical method has been successfully applied to predict and analyze unusual Hall effects resulting from electron spin-orbit interactions and Zeeman effects in magnetic fields. Our model shows that the unusual intrinsic Hall effect can occur up to a third-order of magnetic field strength when the spin-orbit interaction is considered as a key factor. When our model was further developed to account for the effects of other scattering mechanisms, such as electron-impurity interactions and electron-phonon interactions, it was found that the third-order unusual Hall effect can occur under specific conditions of these interactions. To verify the validity of our theoretical model, the results were compared with experimental data from a study on indium arsenide single crystals, and the findings demonstrate a strong correlation between the model's predictions and actual results.

The increasing focus on call graph analysis across various domains such as software modernization and cybersecurity has resulted in a surge of call graphs that need to be examined. Analyzing these call graphs to pinpoint performance or security issues, however, is impeded by the difficulty in comparing a large number of call graphs due to the absence of widely accepted metrics. A novel framework has been developed, incorporating both manual and automated analysis, to identify key characteristics of call graphs, resulting in the creation of a call graph similarity metric. This metric is then utilized in the development of a visualization tool capable of efficiently handling a large number of call graphs. Evaluations of the tool demonstrate its ability to effectively facilitate the comparison of call graphs.

The "No News is Poor News" phenomenon is a common occurrence where news articles are removed from view to conceal sensitive information, but it also poses challenges for Natural Language Processing models in learning from large datasets. However, this research brings attention to a complementary problem, "No News is Positive News," where censored news articles are overrepresented in available text datasets, distorting model performance. To address this, the study examines how text datasets are populated and proposes a method to identify and mitigate news censorship bias. It also proposes a new evaluation metric to assess the impact of different datasets on model performance.

High-resolution X-ray observations have allowed researchers to identify quasi-periodic oscillations in solar flare coronal loops, which can occur when magnetic reconnection is triggered by quasi-periodic fluctuations in the flare current sheet. A new simulation method is presented that combines 2.5-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations with 3.5-dimensional kinetic simulations to study the oscillations in the flare current sheet. The research shows that the microwave polarization of quasi-periodic oscillations is highly dependent on the orientation of the current sheet, resulting in two polarization modes. The first mode is linearly polarized when the current sheet is approximately perpendicular to the ambient magnetic field, while the second mode is circularly polarized when it is parallel to the ambient magnetic field. The oscillations in the flare current sheet can be detected at microwave wavelengths, producing distinct signals with linear or circular polarization. The oscillation period is determined by the time delay between the oscillation in the current sheet and the oscillation in the coronal loop, with longer periods corresponding to larger oscillation periods in the current sheet.

A significant challenge in signal processing involves detecting anomalies within complex data derived from real-world phenomena. A significant amount of research has been dedicated to addressing this issue, particularly in the context of image processing where noise and anomalies can be difficult to distinguish. Various methods have been developed to meet specific application requirements, but they are not typically suited for industrial settings where precise parameter tuning is often a necessity. This work presents a straightforward yet versatile approach for detecting anomalies in signal data, with a particular focus on its practical utility in the oil and gas sector. This novel method is designed to efficiently identify anomalies of diverse types by exploiting the presence of a reference signal, which is often the case in real-world applications. A detailed performance evaluation was conducted using artificially generated signals mimicking real-world scenarios. Furthermore, the method was successfully tested on real-world data collected from a commercial sensor system used in a high-pressure carbon dioxide pipeline.

We investigate the KP-I equation, specifically an modified version that accounts for dispersion, given by the derivative of u in terms of negative fractional derivatives of both time and space variables and the additional factor $\nu\partial_x u$, where $\nu$ is a positive constant. Under the assumption that the solution u has a double integral over space and a double integral over time that is square-integrable, we establish existence and uniqueness of solutions to the KP-I equation, leveraging a transformation that maps the equation to a related NLS equation and applying Strichartz estimates for that equation.

Kramer's relation, stating the doubling of the entropy of a ferromagnetic material's magnetic states due to an applied magnetic field, can be extended to various quantum systems with degenerate states. However, when these systems interact with their environment and lose coherence, Kramer's relation can be violated, leading to possible breaches of entropic degeneracy. The research explores the potential breaches and breaches of Kramer's relation caused by thermal contact and non-thermal interactions between the system and its environment. Additionally, it examines how systems with breached Kramer's relation may experience a revival of degeneracy under specific circumstances, particularly when the interactions with the environment match the system's inherent symmetry, providing insights into the applications of Kramer's relation to various quantum systems.

In highly-mobile MIMO systems, accurately predicting future channel state information (CSI) responses is crucial to minimizing channel training overhead and ensuring seamless connectivity. A novel approach is proposed to address this challenge, leveraging a state-space model and long short-term memory (LSTM) deep learning model that can effectively handle unpredictable and complex CSI dynamics. The proposed LSTM model is particularly well-suited to learning the state-space model's complex dynamics, and its adaptability is demonstrated through its resistance to varying network conditions and different prediction horizons. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated by outperforming traditional methods under various scenarios.

Economic researchers frequently analyze and compare inequality measurements across countries during their normal working hours. However, the availability of data is limited due to the nature of this data which requires consideration of working hours in both time-series and cross-section contexts. This paper introduces an approach that uses a mixture of Beta distribution to estimate inequality measurements from data collected according to working hours. The proposed method's performance is compared with other techniques under different mixture scenarios. Simulation studies reveal that the proposed method yields more accurate results than others, provided the underlying mixture is correctly specified. The method is then applied to study inequality measurements for employed and non-retired individuals in U.S states between 2003-2011.

We establish an asymptotic expansion for the Szeg\H{o} kernel on a Grauert cylinder, which corresponds to a smooth model of a projective variety. Specifically, we obtain an expansion in 1/|\lambda| with respect to a parameter \lambda related to the complex structure of the Grauet cylinder. This analysis is grounded in the use of a quantized sheaf, whose properties are investigated via the resolution of a related deformation problem.

The reverse line graph, a concept first introduced in 1963 by Sabidussa and Sheldon, has since been redefined by Sabidussa and others in 1970s.  A simpler approach to generate the reverse line graph was proposed by Sabidussa and others in 1970s.  A newer, alternative algorithm, developed by Sabidussa and others in the late 1970s, simplifies this earlier approach.  A detailed analysis of the newer algorithm, titled MARINLINGA, was first provided by Sabidussa and others in 1980s.  A comparison between MARINLINGA and Roussopoulos's reverse line graph algorithm, first introduced in 1984, was first made by Sabidussa and others in 1984.  A detailed analysis of the time complexity of MARINLINGA and Roussopoulos's reverse line graph algorithm, as well as a comparison of their respective complexities, was first provided by Sabidussa and others in 1984.  This paper aims to provide a detailed analysis of MARINLINGA and Roussopoulos's reverse line graph algorithm, as well as a detailed analysis of the time complexity comparison between the two, including a detailed analysis of MARINLINGA and Roussopoulos's reverse line graph algorithm, as well as a detailed analysis of the time complexity comparison between the two, including a detailed analysis of MARINLINGA and Roussopoulos's

This paper validates a conjecture put forth by Lee-Lee, which claims that the Lie algebra associated with central extensions of the Galois group in p-adic Hodge theory is flat.
